title: Blood Star
summary: A highest-tier Monster Class spell that works on any monster without Magic resistance. A hit takes a fixed share of the caster's Magic from the foe's vitality rather than rolling a range of harm, and casting costs Health as well as Mana.
standalone_fallback: Use it as a costly signature spell: the caster pays in both Mana and Health to strike any foe that lacks magical resistance, with the harm tied to the caster's own magical strength rather than to chance.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: The Blood Star Spell whips any monster without Magic resistance. Rather than a range of damage, a hit reduces the foe's hit points by a third of the caster's Magic characteristic number, so its strength follows the caster's magical attainment.

sections.heading: Costs & Limits
sections.text: Casting it costs Health as well as Mana, so the caster pays in vitality for every use. It is ineffective on monsters with Magic resistance.

potency.why: A highest-tier spell that reliably harms any non-resistant monster in proportion to the caster's Magic.

range.why: The card gives no range; it is treated as a targeted spell within sight.

cost.why: Casting consumes Health as well as Mana.

facts.cost_narrative: Paid in both Health and Mana on each casting.

title: Bone Spirit
summary: A highest-tier Monster Class spell that strips a large share of a target's remaining vitality with each strike. After a few shots even a formerly tough foe falls quickly. It costs Health as well as Mana.
standalone_fallback: Use it as a costly spirit-bolt that gnaws away a big portion of a foe's remaining strength per hit, paid for in the caster's own blood and magic.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: The Bone Spirit spell reduces a target's Hit Points by a third every time it strikes. After two or three shots even a formerly tough foe can be finished quickly.

sections.heading: Source & Teachers
sections.text: It is a highest-tier spell of the Monster Class.

sections.heading: Costs & Limits
sections.text: Casting it costs the caster Health as well as Mana, a real price for the damage it deals.

potency.why: Each strike takes a large share of the target's remaining vitality, and a few strikes finish a tough foe.

range.why: It strikes a target, but the card gives no range.

cost.why: It consumes the caster's Health as well as Mana.

facts.cost_narrative: The caster pays in both Health and Mana for each casting.
facts.range_note: Strikes a chosen target; range not stated.

title: Chain Lightning
summary: A high-end lightning spell the Sorcerer relies on as the best defense later in the game, found as books in the dungeon.
standalone_fallback: Use it as a late-game offensive caster spell that arcs lightning through enemies, at the cost of draining the caster's magical reserves quickly.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: Chain Lightning is an offensive high-end spell of the lightning school. Bursts of it can be used as a ranged attack against Balrogs.

sections.heading: Source & Teachers
sections.text: It is found as spell books in the dungeon. A Warrior is told to keep an eye out for the books of Stone Curse, Chain Lightning, Inferno, Teleport, and Flame Wave. The Sorcerer casts it.

sections.heading: Costs & Limits
sections.text: It is mana-hungry.

sections.heading: Lore
sections.text: The Sorcerer uses it, along with Stone Curse, Flame Wave and the occasional dose of Elemental, as the best defense later in the game.

potency.why: One of the high-end spells the Sorcerer uses as the best defense later in the game.

range.why: Used as a ranged attack, but the card gives no more detail on its reach.

cost.why: Described as mana-hungry.

facts.cost_narrative: Draws heavily on the caster's mana.
facts.range_note: Ranged bursts; no distance is given.

title: Charged Bolt
summary: A lightning spell that produces multiple projectiles which bounce off walls. It is a poor choice against lightning-resistant creatures, which it may slow but probably will not kill.
standalone_fallback: Use it as a cheap lightning attack that fires several bolts to ricochet around a room. It is weak against anything that resists lightning.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: This spell produces multiple lightning projectiles, which bounce off the walls until they strike a foe or eventually dissipate. A further book adds more bolts as the caster improves.

sections.heading: Costs & Limits
sections.text: The spell asks for only modest magical aptitude and a small amount of mana. Its main limit is lightning resistance. If you throw a Charged Bolt at a lightning-resistant creature, you might slow it down, but you probably won't kill it.

potency.why: Several bouncing bolts are useful in their niche, but they fail against resistant creatures.

range.why: Bolts fly across a room and bounce off walls until they hit or fade.

cost.why: Its mana cost is small among the card's figures.

facts.cost_narrative: A small amount of mana per casting.
facts.range_note: Bolts bounce off walls until they strike a foe or dissipate.

title: Elemental
summary: A high-end Sorcerer offensive spell that does not dissipate over distance and so works well at range.
standalone_fallback: Use it as a ranged elemental attack spell for an experienced caster. It keeps its force over distance, so it suits attacks on distant foes.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: Elemental is one of the high-end spells the Sorcerer uses occasionally as a late-game offense. The guide names it, with Fireball, as a spell that works quite nicely at range because it does not dissipate over distance.

sections.heading: Source & Teachers
sections.text: It comes from the Sorcerer's spell list. The card names no teacher.

potency.why: It is a high-end offensive spell used occasionally, but the card gives no detail on its strength.

range.why: It does not dissipate over distance and works well at range, but the card gives no scale.

cost.why: The card says nothing about its cost, so it is rated Medium by default.

facts.range_note: Does not dissipate over distance, so it works well at range.

title: Fireball
summary: A Sorcerer spell that does not dissipate over distance, so it works well at range.
standalone_fallback: Use it as a long-range blast that a spellcaster can hurl across a room or cavern without losing force. It needs no setting beyond a caster and a distant foe.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: Fireball is one of the Sorcerer's ranged spells. It works well because it does not dissipate over distance.

sections.heading: Source & Teachers
sections.text: It belongs to the Sorcerer's spell list. The guide ranks it as a good option next to the mostly lightning-based spells, with Elemental.

potency.why: Described as working 'quite nicely', so reliable but not singled out as overwhelming.

range.why: It keeps its force over distance, but the card gives no reach beyond line of sight.

cost.why: The card says nothing about its cost.

facts.range_note: Does not dissipate over distance, so it suits long-range use.

title: Firebolt
summary: A basic fire spell that almost every character learns early on.
standalone_fallback: Use it as the simple starter attack spell of any caster: a bolt of fire that gets faster and cheaper with further study.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: Firebolt is a fire attack. Each additional book makes it hit harder and move faster while costing less mana. An Enchanted shrine can raise it.

sections.heading: Source & Teachers
sections.text: No teacher is named. It is an early-game spell learned by almost every character.

sections.heading: Costs & Limits
sections.text: It costs a little mana per casting, and the cost falls with extra books. An Enchanted shrine draws on the caster's mana reserve to raise it.

sections.heading: Lore
sections.text: The guide uses Firebolt as an example of a spell whose effectiveness a Sorcerer should test as experience climbs: a first-level spell that almost every character learns early on.

potency.why: A first-level, early-game spell; it improves with books but stays basic.

range.why: A ranged bolt attack; the card gives no distance.

cost.why: A small mana price that shrinks with extra books.

facts.cost_narrative: A modest mana cost that decreases with each additional book.
facts.range_note: Bolt attack; no distance is stated.

title: Flame Wave
summary: A high-end Sorcerer offensive spell, used once the Sorcerer has advanced. It is found as a spell book in the dungeon.
standalone_fallback: Use it as a late-game fire attack spell for an advanced caster. It is a reward found in a spell book, not something learned early.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: Flame Wave is one of the high-end spells the Sorcerer uses as an offense later in the game.

sections.heading: Source & Teachers
sections.text: It is found as spell books in the dungeon. The guide lists it among the upper-end spells the Warrior should look for, alongside Stone Curse, Chain Lightning, Inferno and Teleport. The Sorcerer casts it.

potency.why: It is a high-end offensive spell, but the card gives no detail on its strength.

range.why: The card says nothing about its range, so it is rated Medium by default.

cost.why: The card says nothing about its cost, so it is rated Medium by default.

title: Golem
summary: A summoned stone ally that hunts enemies. The Sorcerer sends it into a room to draw attacks so that Stone Curse can be placed on the attackers.
standalone_fallback: Use it as a single summoned decoy and hunter that the caster sends ahead. It pulls enemy attention so the caster can act on the enemies while they are distracted.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: The Golem spell gives you a helper who'll seek out your enemies and destroy them. The Sorcerer also uses it as a decoy. Send your Golem into a room and watch for him to come under attack. Then cast Stone Curse over the area of the magic attack until the magic stops. This combination is perhaps the only way for a Sorcerer to triumph over Diablo's minions on Hell difficulty.

sections.heading: Source & Teachers
sections.text: The Sorcerer casts it. The card names no teacher.

sections.heading: Costs & Limits
sections.text: Only one Golem can exist at a time. A second summons replaces the old one. A Golem's toughness is based on the caster's mana and spell skill.

potency.why: The card calls its combination with Stone Curse perhaps the only way to beat Diablo's minions on the hardest difficulty.

range.why: The Golem is sent into a room ahead of the caster and watched from a distance.

cost.why: It uses mana and only one can exist at a time. The card names no lasting price.

facts.cost_narrative: Mana is spent to summon it. Only one Golem exists at a time, and its toughness depends on the caster's mana and spell skill.
facts.range_note: Sent ahead into a room, where it seeks out enemies on its own.

title: Heal Other
summary: A multiplayer spell that heals a weary comrade. The caster highlights the target, then right-clicks to restore their health.
standalone_fallback: Use it as a spell that lets one character mend an ally they can see, at a cost to the caster's magical reserves. It suits any party with a healer.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: Heal Other restores health to another character. The caster highlights the target to see their current vitality, then right-clicks to heal.

sections.heading: Source & Teachers
sections.text: It is available in multiplayer only and is learned from a spell book. It requires a fairly high level of magical aptitude.

sections.heading: Costs & Limits
sections.text: It draws on the caster's mana, and the price grows with the spell's mastery. Extra book study increases the healing and lowers the mana cost a little.

potency.why: It reliably restores an ally, but the card does not call it decisive.

range.why: The target must be highlighted, so it works within sight.

cost.why: A mana price that scales with mastery.

facts.cost_narrative: Costs mana, with the price rising with spell mastery; further study improves healing and eases the cost.
facts.range_note: Within sight, since the target must be highlighted.

title: Healing
summary: A restorative spell cast by the Sorcerer that heals the caster at the cost of Mana. Best used outside combat, with stockpiled scrolls covering battle.
standalone_fallback: A caster can mend their own wounds by spending magical energy. Use it between fights, and keep consumable scrolls for the heat of battle.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: Heals the caster and restores Health. Further study of the spell's book improves the healing while lowering the Mana it demands.

sections.heading: Source & Teachers
sections.text: The spell is a Sorcerer's practice, learned from a book. The card names Pepin and Adria as sources of Scrolls of Healing, which the Sorcerer is advised to stockpile for use in battle.

sections.heading: Costs & Limits
sections.text: It costs Mana. Burning Mana during combat is not advised for Sorcerers, who should use stockpiled Scrolls of Healing in battle and cast with Mana outside combat. The guide notes that "Generally, it's best to go that route, and heal with Mana when you're not in the heat of battle." The spell becomes Mana-efficient for the Sorcerer at some point, which makes the choice more drastic.

potency.why: Reliably restores Health for its caster, a decisive niche role, though it is not described as turning fights.

range.why: It heals the caster only.

cost.why: Costs Mana, a noticeable price that makes it unwise mid-combat, but it grows more efficient with study.

facts.cost_narrative: Paid in Mana; costly enough in battle that scrolls are preferred there, and it grows cheaper with further book study.
facts.range_note: Heals the caster only.

title: Identify
summary: A spell, available only through scroll or staff, that reveals the nature of magical objects, which may help or harm their owner.
standalone_fallback: A consumable charm or scroll reveals what a magical object truly does, so the party can tell blessings from curses without a trip back to town.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: This important spell determines the nature of magical objects: not all magical items assist your persona, and some may even cause you harm.

sections.heading: Source & Teachers
sections.text: It comes from scroll and staff only. Adria sells it, and she generally carries a Scroll of Identify. The guide advises buying them whenever they appear, so the player need not return to Tristram to check an item. Cain the Storyteller is also tied to the service.

sections.heading: Costs & Limits
sections.text: It cannot be learned from a book, so it depends on finding or buying scrolls and staves. The card gives it no Mana cost.

potency.why: Reliably decisive in its niche of vetting magical items, but it does not act on the world.

range.why: Applies to an object being examined; the card states no wider reach.

cost.why: Its Mana figure is zero; the cost is acquiring the scroll.

facts.cost_narrative: No Mana is spent; the price is obtaining a scroll or staff.
facts.range_note: Applied to a single magical object.

title: Inferno
summary: A high-level fire spell whose area and efficiency grow with the caster's experience, far more impressive for a Sorcerer than a Warrior.
standalone_fallback: Use it as a fire spell whose area grows as its caster advances. A dedicated mage commands a large blaze, while a martial character gets only a modest one.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: Inferno is a fire spell. Combat spells grow in area of effect and mana efficiency as they increase in level, and a high-level Sorcerer's Inferno covers a large area.

sections.heading: Source & Teachers
sections.text: It is found as spell books in the dungeon. The Warrior is told to keep an eye out for the books of Stone Curse, Chain Lightning, Inferno, Teleport, and Flame Wave. No teacher is named.

sections.heading: Lore
sections.text: The guide stresses how different the spell is in the hands of a Sorcerer and a Warrior who have both advanced a long way. The Sorcerer's version is far more impressive.

potency.why: Described as amazing in a Sorcerer's hands, with an area that grows with level.

range.why: An area effect that grows with the caster, but no distance is given.

cost.why: The card gives no specific cost beyond mana; efficiency improves with advancement.

facts.cost_narrative: Costs mana, becoming more efficient as the caster advances.
facts.range_note: Area grows with the caster's advancement; no distance is stated.

title: Infravision
summary: Lets the caster see through walls, showing lurking monsters in a reddish hue. It is seldom a significant tactical advantage, except when lining up a Wall of Fire. Scroll only.
standalone_fallback: Use it as a one-off scouting charm that reveals hidden creatures behind walls as red shapes. It helps most when the caster plans an area attack.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: The Infravision spell allows the caster to see through walls, displaying lurking monsters in a reddish hue.

sections.heading: Source & Teachers
sections.text: It is found on scrolls only.

sections.heading: Costs & Limits
sections.text: It is seldom a significant tactical advantage. It helps mainly when lining up a Wall of Fire.

potency.why: Seldom a significant tactical advantage, useful mainly in specific situations.

range.why: It shows monsters beyond walls, within a scene.

cost.why: The card gives no cost.

facts.range_note: Reveals monsters behind walls nearby.

title: Lightning
summary: A Sorcerer spell that does not dissipate over distance and outranges Poison Spitter spitting, but is useless against lightning-immune demons.
standalone_fallback: Use it as a caster's long-range bolt that nothing can outdistance. Creatures immune to lightning force the caster to pick another approach.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: Lightning is a single-target stream whose bolt grows longer as the spell advances. It does not dissipate over distance, so the Sorcerer can use it to outdistance the spitting of Poison Spitters. Chain lightning bursts are a related use.

sections.heading: Source & Teachers
sections.text: It is on the Sorcerer's spell list. No teacher is named.

sections.heading: Costs & Limits
sections.text: It costs mana, and extra books reduce the cost. It has no effect on lightning-immune creatures such as Red Storm, so a Sorcerer needs an alternative against them.

sections.heading: Lore
sections.text: The guide notes that Lightning provides unlimited range, though poison balls fall to the ground after a certain distance.

potency.why: Reliable at range in its niche, but wholly ineffective against lightning-immune foes.

range.why: The guide says it provides unlimited range.

cost.why: A mana cost that falls with extra books; no other price is named.

facts.cost_narrative: Costs mana, and extra books reduce the cost.

counters.original: Red Storm are immune to lightning; a Sorcerer needs an alternative

facts.range_note: Unlimited range; the bolt lengthens as the spell advances.

title: Mana Shield
summary: A protective spell, learned from a book or bought as a scroll, that lets magical reserves absorb harm in place of life.
standalone_fallback: Use it as a protective spell that makes the caster's magical reserve a second health pool. It lapses whenever the caster travels between places.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: Mana Shield allows the caster to utilize Mana points as Hit Points, drawing off of Mana instead of health when damage is sustained in combat. For every level of Mana Shield, the damage taken is reduced. For a Sorcerer it is effectively essential. With it, a large magical reserve can stand in for a small store of life, which is why vitality matters to Sorcerers only early in the game.

sections.heading: Source & Teachers
sections.text: It is learned from a book of Mana Shield, or bought as a Mana Shield Scroll sold by Adria the Witch in Tristram. The Sorcerer and the Rogue both use it, and the guide advises buying a scroll whenever one appears in the Witch's inventory and counting yourself lucky to find a book.

sections.heading: Costs & Limits
sections.text: The cost is mana, drawn in place of health. The spell wears off when the caster moves between levels or returns to town, so it has to be recast before every significant chunk of adventuring. Without the spell itself, scrolls are a constant need.

sections.heading: Lore
sections.text: The guide calls it almost as important for the Rogue as for the Sorcerer. Experience poured into Magic early can pay off greatly through Mana Shield.

potency.why: Effectively essential for the Sorcerer; the large magical reserve becomes a durable second pool of protection.

range.why: It protects the caster only.

cost.why: Paid in mana drawn in place of health, and the spell lapses on travel.

facts.cost_narrative: Damage is paid from mana instead of health, and the spell must be recast after moving between levels or going to town.
facts.range_note: Self only.

title: Nova
summary: A devastating radial Lightning attack found only on scrolls and staffs. It is so powerful that even a Sorcerer cannot learn it from a book.
standalone_fallback: Treat it as a rare one-use or item-bound lightning burst that strikes all around the wielder. Whoever finds the scroll or staff gets a story-turning blast.

sections.text: Nova is a radial Lightning attack. It strikes outward from the caster and is described as devastating.

sections.heading: Source & Teachers
sections.text: It is available only from scrolls and staffs. It cannot be learned from a book, even by a Sorcerer.

sections.heading: Costs & Limits
sections.text: The main limit is access. It cannot be learned and exists only in scroll or staff form, so the user needs the right item.

sections.heading: Lore

summary: Teleports the caster in a random direction. It is hard to aim and wasteful of Mana, so the guide recommends it for leaping across dungeon sections or escaping swarms.

sections.heading: Costs & Limits

potency.why: Reliably useful for escape, but unpredictable.

range.why: Moves the caster within a scene; no distance is given.

cost.why: Described as wasteful of Mana, but not as a lasting price.

facts.cost_narrative: Wasteful of mana, with no control over where the caster lands.

title: Resurrect
summary: A multiplayer-only spell, available through staff and scroll, that raises a dead ally who returns barely alive.
standalone_fallback: A rare scroll can call a fallen companion back, but they return on the brink of death. Use it only once the area is safe.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: Raises a dead ally. The raised character returns with only one Hit Point, though further book study is noted to give more.

sections.heading: Source & Teachers
sections.text: Available from scroll and staff only, and only in multiplayer. "Just in case, Pepin always has a Resurrect scroll in his inventory during multiplayer games."

sections.heading: Costs & Limits
sections.text: The spell leaves the raised ally nearly dead. "Using the spell only gives the raised character one Hit Point, so don't do it in hostile territory unless you're prepared to cast." It also takes a considerable outlay of Mana and a hard-to-find scroll or staff.

potency.why: Returns a dead ally to play, which can turn the course of a fight, though the ally is left fragile.

range.why: Targets a fallen ally in the scene; the card gives no range.

cost.why: Its Mana outlay is notable and the result is fragile, but the card describes no lasting price.

facts.range_note: Targets a dead ally; no range is stated.

title: Sorcerer Staff Recharging
summary: The Sorcerer's innate ability to recharge staves, analogous to the Warrior's repair skill.
standalone_fallback: A spellcaster can restore the charges of a magical staff, though each recharge leaves the staff able to hold less than before.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: The Sorcerer possesses the ability to recharge staves, an ability analogous to the Warrior's repair. It improves with experience.

sections.heading: Source & Teachers

cost.why: The upper-end Charges number lowers with experience-linked recharging; the card is otherwise silent, so this is judged.

title: Stone Curse
summary: A high-end spell that petrifies enemies over an area, even without line of sight, so they cannot flee and shatter under a few weapon blows.
standalone_fallback: Use it as a caster's signature control spell. It freezes a group of foes in stone for a short time, and allies can then smash them with ordinary weapons.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: Stone Curse is the most effective way to keep enemies from running away. It works on an area, and no line of sight is needed. Targets are petrified for a time. Once stoned, a few whacks with any weapon on hand is usually all it takes to reduce the dark ones to rubble. It can also be tried as a ranged attack against Balrogs, though that is described as a matter of luck.

sections.heading: Source & Teachers
sections.text: The card does not say who teaches it. It is one of the upper-end spells a Warrior is told to look for as books in the dungeon, and it is a Sorcerer spell that the Rogue can also cast.

sections.heading: Costs & Limits
sections.text: The caster must be close, and the petrification is temporary. Because of this, it is best paired with something that finishes the targets while they are stoned.

sections.heading: Lore
sections.text: The guide calls Stone Curse and a decent bow a deadly combination for the Rogue. Paired with the Golem, it is perhaps the only way for a Sorcerer to triumph over Diablo's minions on Hell difficulty.

potency.why: Called the most effective way to stop fleeing enemies and a deadly combination with a bow or Golem.

range.why: Works over an area without line of sight, but the caster must be close.

cost.why: The card names only closeness and temporariness as limits and gives no other price, so a normal casting cost is assumed.

facts.cost_narrative: The card names no explicit price beyond the caster having to be close and the effect being temporary.
facts.range_note: Area effect that needs no line of sight, but the caster must be close.

title: Telekinesis
summary: A spell that lets the caster manipulate distant objects with the mind. The Rogue uses it to open doors from afar and fire arrows through the opening.
standalone_fallback: Use it as a minor utility power that opens doors, chests and sarcophagi from a distance. It can also shove a monster back, which lets an archer shoot through the gap.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: This spell allows the caster to manipulate distant objects with the power of the mind. It opens chests, sarcophagi and doors, and it pushes monsters back. The Rogue can open doors with Telekinesis and fire arrows through the portal from a distance.

sections.heading: Source & Teachers
sections.text: The card names the Rogue as the caster. It gives no teacher.

sections.heading: Costs & Limits
sections.text: The spell needs a fair measure of magical aptitude and spends mana on each use. Its effect is utility and displacement, not damage. The Sorcerer is advised to use Teleport rather than Telekinesis to escape crowds.

potency.why: It opens things and pushes monsters back, which is situational help rather than a decisive effect.

range.why: It works on distant objects within sight, so the Rogue can act from a distance.

cost.why: It has a mana cost and a magic requirement. The card gives no other price.

facts.cost_narrative: Mana is spent each time, and the caster needs enough magical aptitude to learn it.
facts.range_note: Works on distant objects, so doors can be opened from afar.

title: Town Portal
summary: A spell that opens a gateway between the dungeon and a spot just outside Tristram's town square. It lets the caster return to town quickly and come back to the exact point they left.
standalone_fallback: Use it as a reliable escape-and-resupply gate in any delve. The portal leads to a safe hub and returns the party to the exact spot where it was opened.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: Town Portal is the quickest route back to town short of taking the stairs. It opens a direct gateway to a spot just outside Tristram's town square. The trip runs both ways. It allows access to the town, then a return to the dungeon from the exact point where the spell was cast. It is useful for all classes, and the guide calls it an indispensable way to return to town without a lot of tedious leg-work.

sections.heading: Source & Teachers
sections.text: Adria the Witch keeps a steady supply of Town Portal spells. They are always available in scroll form from her, which makes the Town Portal the primary means of travel between the dungeon and Tristram.

sections.heading: Costs & Limits
sections.text: The spell is used in scroll form, so each casting uses up a scroll bought from Adria. Extra scrolls found in the dungeon can pile up. The guide advises throwing them on the ground in Tristram near where the portal opens and picking them up on the next return to town.

potency.why: It reliably solves the problem of getting back to town, but it does nothing in a fight.

range.why: It links the dungeon to the town and back, crossing the whole distance between them.

cost.why: Scrolls are always available from Adria and the card names no other price.

facts.cost_narrative: Each use spends a scroll bought from Adria the Witch. Spare scrolls can be stashed on the ground in Tristram.
facts.range_note: Links the dungeon caster's position to a spot just outside Tristram's town square, and back to the exact casting point.

title: Wall of Fire
summary: A fire spell listed in the spell index with a modest Magic requirement from scrolls or staves and a higher one from a book. Book study lengthens its duration and eases its Mana cost, and infravision helps line it up.
standalone_fallback: Use it as a fire barrier a caster raises to block or punish passage, easier to cast from a scroll or staff than from a book, and best aimed with good sight in the dark.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: Wall of Fire is a fire spell listed in the spell index. Its book effects lengthen its duration and reduce its Mana cost.

sections.heading: Source & Teachers
sections.text: It can be learned from a book, which demands a higher Magic attainment, or used from a scroll or staff, which demands a lower one. Infravision is noted as useful for lining up a Wall of Fire.

sections.heading: Costs & Limits
sections.text: It draws on Mana, a fraction of the caster's current level. Reading from a book eases that Mana price, and the spell needs a real Magic attainment before it can be used at all.

potency.why: The card gives no damage detail; a fire spell with lasting effect is judged reliable in its niche.

range.why: The card gives no range; infravision for lining it up implies a placed effect within sight.

cost.why: A noticeable Mana price, reduced by book effects.

facts.cost_narrative: A moderate Mana price, eased by book study.
facts.range_note: Aimed by sight; infravision helps line it up.

title: Warrior Repair Skill
summary: The Warrior's innate skill of repairing weapons and armor in the field, measured by an item's Durability.
standalone_fallback: A fighter can patch up weapons and armor in the field, but each item wears down for good over time and vanishes when it has nothing left.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: Repairs weapons and armor in the field, measured by the item's Durability number. The skill grows with each level of experience, so the more experienced the Warrior, the more effective the repairs.

sections.heading: Source & Teachers
sections.text: An innate ability of the Warrior; no teacher is named.

sections.heading: Costs & Limits
sections.text: Repairs lower the upper-end Durability number of the item, and an item vanishes when its Durability reaches zero. Repair is therefore a lasting trade-off, not a free restoration.

potency.why: Reliably useful for keeping gear working, but it only slows decline.

range.why: Works on an item the Warrior handles.

cost.why: Each repair lowers the item's maximum Durability, a lasting but gradual price.

facts.cost_narrative: Each repair lowers the item's upper-end Durability, and an item vanishes at zero.
facts.range_note: Touch-level work on one item.

title: Brotherhood of the Vizjerei
summary: An order of magic-users to which the Sorcerer belongs.
standalone_fallback: Use them as an order of scholarly spellcasters whose members are skilled with scrolls and spells. A member can appear as a patron, mentor or rival to any magic-using character.

sections.heading: Philosophy & Goals
sections.text: The source says only that the Brotherhood is an order of magic-users. Its members are described as especially adept at utilizing scrolls and spells. No goals are stated.

sections.heading: Structure & Ranks
sections.text: No structure or ranks are given. The Sorcerer is a member, and nothing more about the Brotherhood is given in this Section.

sections.heading: Using them in play
sections.text: Use the Brotherhood as a light framework for a sorcerer's training and loyalties. Its allies, rivals, base and internal workings are not stated, so the GM must supply them to suit the campaign.

reach.why: The card says nothing about reach; rated Medium by default.

force.why: Members are skilled with spells, but no numbers or forces are described; judged by default.

wealth.why: The card says nothing about wealth; rated Medium by default.

secrecy.why: The card says nothing about secrecy; rated Medium by default.

title: Sisters of the Sightless Eye
summary: A mysterious order to which the Rogue belongs, whose members have a sixth sense for perceiving and disarming traps before they spring.
standalone_fallback: Use them as a secretive sisterhood of scouts and infiltrators whose members can sense and defuse traps before they trigger. Any party delving into a trapped site can meet one as a guide, rival or recruiter.

sections.heading: Philosophy & Goals
sections.text: The order is described as mysterious. The only thing the text establishes about its outlook is a gift: a "sixth sense" that lets its members perceive and disarm traps before they spring. Its wider aims are not stated.

sections.heading: Structure & Ranks
sections.text: The text gives no ranks or hierarchy. It names the Rogue as one of the Sisters, so the order has individual members who go out into the world.

sections.heading: Using them in play
sections.text: Treat the Sisters as a hook rather than a developed organisation. A member can serve as an uncanny trap-finder for the party, and the order's mystery is left open for the GM to fill in. Details such as the order's base, leadership and motives are not in the source and are the GM's to decide.

reach.why: The card says nothing about the order's reach; rated Medium by default.

force.why: Only a single member is named and no fighting strength is described.

wealth.why: The card says nothing about wealth; rated Medium by default.

title: Balrog Weakness Hint
summary: A veteran's piece of guidance says fire resistance should be a priority, because the Balrogs will soon give the player reason enough to seek it.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-shot briefing scene. A veteran warns the party that the demons ahead burn what they touch, and the party has one chance to find fire protection before the first Balrog encounter.
premise: A party that prepares for the wrong dangers + a foe that punishes them for it = a scramble for fire protection before the first burning blow.

sensory.physical_environment: Scorched stone, heat shimmer and the glow of flame in corridors that should be cold.
sensory.behaviors: Veterans check their gear for fire protection first and talk about the Balrogs in lowered voices.
sensory.relationships: The advisor is a mentor to the party. The Balrogs are the looming predator behind the advice.
sensory.attitudes: Wary pragmatism. Fire is treated as the thing that will eventually find you.
sensory.values: Preparation over bravado, and knowledge passed on before it is needed.

establishment.name: The veteran guide
establishment.worldview: Survival comes from preparing for what is coming, not what is comfortable.
establishment.leverage: Hard-won experience and a trusted voice.
establishment.flaw: Advice arrives as a hint, not a guarantee, and the party may ignore it.

main_opponent.name: The Balrogs
main_opponent.worldview: Burn everything that enters their domain.
main_opponent.leverage: Fire damage that punishes unprepared characters.
main_opponent.flaw: Their strength is a single dominant element, which makes them predictable to counter.

thematic_shadow.name: The overconfident hero
thematic_shadow.worldview: Strength and weapons alone will carry the day.
thematic_shadow.leverage: Momentum and boldness.
thematic_shadow.flaw: Ignores protection until it is too late.

tertiary_outcast.name: A scavenger who trades in protective gear
tertiary_outcast.worldview: Every danger is a market.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: Access to rare wards and resistances.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: Prices rise as the danger becomes obvious.

output_dial.level_1: A passing warning is shared, and the party notes fire as a future concern.
output_dial.level_2: Balrogs are sighted or rumored, and the party actively looks for fire protection.
output_dial.level_3: A Balrog strikes an unprepared party, and flames force retreat and costly improvisation.
output_dial.level_4: A party without fire protection is overwhelmed, and the burning dead and lost gear end the expedition.

threat_clocks.name: Balrog Contact
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party descends deeper without gaining fire protection, or ignores signs of Balrog activity.

yields_resource: Fire-ward gear or knowledge and the confidence to face Balrogs with a fighting chance.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: The guide's advice is simple: seek fire resistance, because the Balrogs will make the need plain. The drama is whether the party heeds a quiet warning before a loud one arrives.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place it before the first Balrog territory, at a camp, a vendor or a mentor scene. It consumes the party's preparation time and resources and feeds into fire-ward supply and Balrog encounters. It goes well when the party gathers protection and the first fight is hard but fair. It goes badly when the hint is ignored and the first Balrog turns the encounter into a rout.

title: Blood Fountain
summary: A fountain in the dungeon from which a single drink restores a character's Health. A small refuge of recovery amid the depths.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a quiet oasis room in any dungeon: a fountain of blood-red liquid offers healing to whoever dares drink, and the only question is whether the party takes the offer, shares it, or guards it against others who also need it.
premise: A wounded delver who trusts anything that heals + a fountain that offers recovery without explanation = a gamble between relief and unknown cost.

sensory.physical_environment: A fountain set within the dungeon, its contents offered for drinking.
sensory.behaviors: Wounded characters stop to drink and recover before pressing on.
sensory.relationships: Travelers who share the find, or compete over it, when several are hurt.
sensory.attitudes: Relief mixed with wariness at drinking from a fountain in a dungeon.
sensory.values: Restoration of Health and the chance to continue the descent.

establishment.name: The party's healer or caretaker
establishment.worldview: Recovery is a resource to be rationed so everyone can keep going.
establishment.leverage: Controls who drinks and in what order.
establishment.flaw: Rationing slows the group and breeds resentment.

main_opponent.name: A rival delver or wandering horde claiming the fountain
main_opponent.worldview: Whoever holds the healing wins the dungeon.
main_opponent.leverage: Can contest or foul the fountain and punish those who linger.
main_opponent.flaw: Overconfidence in a place they treat as safe.

thematic_shadow.name: A desperate wounded survivor
thematic_shadow.worldview: Any cure is worth any risk.
thematic_shadow.leverage: Shows what drinking costs when it is relied on too heavily.
thematic_shadow.flaw: Dependence blinds them to danger.

tertiary_outcast.name: A wary scout who refuses to drink
tertiary_outcast.worldview: Nothing in the dungeon is free.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: Notices signs others miss around the fountain.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: Suspicion leaves them weaker than their companions.

output_dial.level_1: The fountain is a calm, untouched stop where a drink eases the party's wounds before they move on.
output_dial.level_2: The fountain helps, but the party must stop, guard it and decide who drinks first.
output_dial.level_3: Rivals or monsters converge on the fountain just as the party is badly hurt and desperate for it.
output_dial.level_4: The party stakes everything on the fountain and finds it contested, fouled or out of reach when the worst moment arrives.

threat_clocks.name: Dependence on the Fountain
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party chooses to push on wounded rather than rest elsewhere, counting on returning to drink.

threat_clocks.name: Rivals Close In
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party lingers, makes noise or leaves signs of their presence near the fountain.

yields_resource: Restored Health for the party, and a fixed point of safety to plan a descent around.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: The Blood Fountain is a single, simple promise: drink and your character's Health is restored. Its value is in the timing. A wounded party that finds it feels relief, and the story is in what they do with it, whether they share, guard or squander it.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place it after a hard fight or hazard, or just before a chokepoint or boss. It consumes the party's time and attention and feeds their ability to continue. It pairs well with chokepoints such as lava crossings and with any pressure from pursuers. An arrival goes well when the party is hurt, calm and cooperative and drinks without incident. It goes badly when they arrive with enemies on their heels, or when they build a plan around the fountain that the situation then denies them. The card gives no further properties, so any hidden cost, limits or guardians are the GM's own addition.

title: The Butcher and the Grated Door
summary: After the party clears the cathedral depths, it lures the Butcher to a doorway flanked by steel grating, closes the door on him, shoots him with a bow until he dies, then takes his Cleaver.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-shot tactical puzzle. A relentless brute cannot be fought in melee, but a doorway with a grated view lets one ranged attacker whittle it down safely, if the party can bait it there.
premise: A party that cannot match a brute in melee + a door the brute cannot pass = a kill from safety and a prize from the corpse.

sensory.physical_environment: A doorway flanked by steel grating, with a closed door between hunter and hunted.
sensory.behaviors: The party baits the Butcher to the doorway, shuts the door in his face and fires from behind the grating.
sensory.relationships: The party relies on terrain against an enemy it could not beat directly.
sensory.attitudes: Patient, calculating and cautious.
sensory.values: Cleverness and preparation beat brute force.

establishment.name: The cleared cathedral depths
establishment.worldview: Order has been restored, and only the Butcher remains.
establishment.leverage: A secured route and room to set up a trap.
establishment.flaw: One mistake brings the Butcher into melee range.

main_opponent.name: The Butcher
main_opponent.worldview: Chase and slaughter whatever moves.
main_opponent.leverage: Overwhelming strength in close combat.
main_opponent.flaw: He chases blindly and cannot get past a closed door.

thematic_shadow.name: The reckless duelist
thematic_shadow.worldview: Honor means facing a foe head-on.
thematic_shadow.leverage: Bravery and a direct approach.
thematic_shadow.flaw: Dies to a brute that cleverness would have beaten.

tertiary_outcast.name: The archer who stays behind the grating
tertiary_outcast.worldview: Distance is the best armor.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: A safe angle and steady ranged fire.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: Depends entirely on the door holding and on having enough ammunition.

output_dial.level_1: The party notes the grated doorway and plans a lure.
output_dial.level_2: The party baits the Butcher to the door, closes it and fires until he falls, then takes the Cleaver.
output_dial.level_3: The bait works but the party's ammunition or nerve falters, and the fight drags on with real risk.
output_dial.level_4: The plan fails, the Butcher reaches the party in the open, and the slaughter the townsman described repeats itself.

threat_clocks.name: The Butcher Closes In
threat_clocks.advances_when: The lure is botched, the party is caught away from the doorway, or ranged fire runs short.

yields_resource: The Butcher's Cleaver, a cleared route onward, and the promise to the dying townsman kept.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: The solution is to let the Butcher chase the party to the grated doorway, close the door in his face and shoot him with a bow until he dies. It rewards using terrain over force.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place it after the surrounding depths are cleared and before the Butcher's room is opened. It consumes ranged equipment and the party's preparation, and it feeds into the Cleaver as loot and into the avenging of the cathedral dead. It goes well when the party spots the doorway and plans around it. It goes badly when the party opens the Butcher's room first and has to improvise against a brute that outmatches it in the open.

title: A Dying Plea at the Desecrated Cathedral
summary: At the cathedral entrance a dying townsman tells the player that Archbishop Lazarus led them into a trap set by a demon called the Butcher, and begs the player to avenge them.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-shot scene. The party meets a dying survivor at a defiled church door, hears who betrayed his group and what killed them, and chooses whether to take up his dying request.
premise: A hero who cannot ignore the dying + a betrayal that cost a whole expedition = a vow to hunt the Butcher and expose the Archbishop.

sensory.physical_environment: A defiled church entrance, with a wounded man slumped near the threshold.
sensory.behaviors: The townsman pleads, accuses and begs to be heard before he dies.
sensory.relationships: Followers were led into a trap by the leader they trusted, and the survivor now turns to a stranger.
sensory.attitudes: Betrayal, despair and a need for vengeance.
sensory.values: Justice for the dead and rest for souls that cannot find it.

establishment.name: Archbishop Lazarus
establishment.worldview: The expedition for the lost prince justifies any cost.
establishment.leverage: Religious authority and the trust of the townsfolk.
establishment.flaw: He led his followers into a trap and is accused of betraying them.

main_opponent.name: The Butcher
main_opponent.worldview: Slaughter whatever enters his domain.
main_opponent.leverage: A demon's brutality that killed the whole expedition.
main_opponent.flaw: He is a single, localized threat that can be hunted down.

thematic_shadow.name: The silent dead of the expedition
thematic_shadow.worldview: They want rest and cannot get it.
thematic_shadow.leverage: The moral weight of unavenged souls.
thematic_shadow.flaw: They have no voice except the survivor's plea.

tertiary_outcast.name: The Wounded Townsman
tertiary_outcast.worldview: Someone must know what happened here.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: First-hand testimony as the last survivor.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: He is dying, and his account is passionate and one-sided.

output_dial.level_1: The townsman is found and heard, and the party notes the accusation.
output_dial.level_2: The party accepts the request, and the Butcher and Lazarus become active leads.
output_dial.level_3: The townsman dies before the full story is told, and the party is left with rumor and a growing sense of betrayal.
output_dial.level_4: The party ignores the plea or descends unprepared, and the Butcher's trap closes on them as it did on the expedition.

threat_clocks.name: Souls Left Unrested
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party delays the hunt, or the cathedral's horrors spread while the Butcher goes unchallenged.

yields_resource: A clear objective, the Butcher, and a damning account of Archbishop Lazarus that gives the party moral standing.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: The dying townsman says the Archbishop led his group down to find the lost prince, that it was a trap, and that everyone was killed by a demon called the Butcher. He asks to be avenged so that the souls of the dead may rest.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place it at the first approach to the desecrated cathedral, as the opening beat of the descent. It consumes the party's curiosity about the church and feeds the Butcher hunt and any Lazarus storyline. It goes well when the plea gives the party a personal stake. It goes badly if the party treats the townsman as set dressing and enters the depths with no sense of the danger or the betrayal behind it.

title: The Catacombs
summary: A dungeon area where Horned Demons are a particular bane.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-shot: the party explores a tomb-like dungeon region where a single kind of horned demon is the greatest threat, and must find a way to get through or around them.
premise: Delvers who press deeper + a region dominated by Horned Demons = survival that depends on handling the one foe that defines the place.

sensory.physical_environment: A dungeon area of catacombs, with Horned Demons dwelling within.
sensory.behaviors: Horned Demons prowl the passages and threaten those who enter.
sensory.relationships: Horned Demons are found in the Catacombs and the Catacombs contain them.
sensory.attitudes: The demons are regarded as the bane of the place.
sensory.values: Caution and preparation over bravado; the dominant threat must be respected.

establishment.name: The Horned Demons
establishment.worldview: They hold the Catacombs as their domain and are its defining presence.
establishment.leverage: Numbers and ferocity within their territory.
establishment.flaw: Bound to one area and a recognizable pattern of threat.

main_opponent.name: Delving party
main_opponent.worldview: Intruders who must cross the Catacombs to progress.
main_opponent.leverage: Planning, tactics and the ability to retreat.
main_opponent.flaw: Outmatched if caught unprepared by the demons.

thematic_shadow.name: Earlier victims
thematic_shadow.worldview: Those who entered before and fell, serving as a warning.
thematic_shadow.leverage: Remains that hint at the demons' habits.
thematic_shadow.flaw: They are already lost.

tertiary_outcast.name: Lone survivor
tertiary_outcast.worldview: Someone who has evaded the demons and wants out more than victory.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: Knowledge of safer routes.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: Shaken, weak and distrustful.

output_dial.level_1: The Catacombs are quiet, with the demons' presence suggested only by signs and distant sounds.
output_dial.level_2: Horned Demons appear in the passages and the party must fight or avoid them with care.
output_dial.level_3: The demons press the party from several directions and withdrawal becomes difficult.
output_dial.level_4: The Catacombs belong entirely to the demons, and the party is trapped, hunted and overwhelmed.

threat_clocks.name: The Demons Close In
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party makes noise, lingers, or leaves demons alive behind them.

yields_resource: Safe passage through the dungeon region and the removal of its defining danger.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: "The Horned Demons are the bane of the Catacombs." The area is defined by a single dominant threat, and the party's success depends on dealing with it.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place it mid-dungeon as a region that tests preparation. It consumes the party's resources and feeds progress deeper into the dungeon. An arrival goes well when the party scouts, plans and fights on chosen ground. It goes badly when they stumble in tired and split, letting the demons dictate the encounter.

title: Catacombs Mausoleum
summary: A mausoleum in the catacombs that opens when the party arrives, letting them return to town from that level.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-shot: deep in a catacomb, a sealed mausoleum opens and offers the party a way back to the surface, at the risk of what slumbers in the tombs around it.
premise: Delvers who need a way out + a mausoleum that opens only once they reach the catacombs = escape that depends on how far they have gone.

sensory.physical_environment: A mausoleum within the catacombs that opens on the party's arrival.
sensory.behaviors: Delvers reach the catacombs and the mausoleum opens to let them return to town.
sensory.relationships: It sits within the Cursed Cathedral's depths and connects that level to Tristram.
sensory.attitudes: Wary gratitude at an exit that appears only after progress.
sensory.values: Passage earned by descent, and the link between the sacred ruin and the town.

establishment.name: The Cursed Cathedral
establishment.worldview: The ruin holds its passages and decides who may use them.
establishment.leverage: The mausoleum opens only once delvers reach the catacombs.
establishment.flaw: It is corrupted and cannot guarantee safe passage.

main_opponent.name: The catacombs' dead
main_opponent.worldview: The tombs are theirs and intruders do not leave.
main_opponent.leverage: They crowd the approach to the mausoleum.
main_opponent.flaw: They are tied to the catacombs and cannot easily follow past it.

thematic_shadow.name: Tristram
thematic_shadow.worldview: The town at the far end of the passage needs delvers to return alive.
thematic_shadow.leverage: Offers rest and supply at the end of the route.
thematic_shadow.flaw: Passive and unable to help those still in the catacombs.

tertiary_outcast.name: A lost delver in the catacombs
tertiary_outcast.worldview: Any exit is worth trusting when the tombs close in.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: Knows where the mausoleum lies.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: Desperate and easily misled.

output_dial.level_1: The mausoleum opens as the party arrives and the way to town is clear.
output_dial.level_2: The mausoleum is open but the route to it is watched and the party must fight or sneak through.
output_dial.level_3: The approach is contested by the catacombs' dead and retreat becomes a costly dash.
output_dial.level_4: The exit is cut off or compromised and the party is trapped in the catacombs with no safe route home.

threat_clocks.name: Tombs Awaken
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party lingers near the mausoleum, makes noise, or disturbs the catacombs' dead.

yields_resource: A reliable return path from the catacombs to town for recovery and resupply.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: When the party reaches the catacombs, the mausoleum opens so they can return to town from that level. It rewards progress with a way home and ties the Cursed Cathedral's depths to Tristram.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place it at the point where the party first enters the catacombs. It consumes the party's momentum and tempts them to retreat, and feeds scenes in Tristram and the Cathedral. An arrival goes well when the party reaches it intact and uses it to regroup. It goes badly when the route is contested, or when the party treats it as a guarantee and is caught by what stirs in the tombs.

title: Cave near Wirt's Clearing
summary: A cave near where Wirt stands in Tristram; the stairs from the ninth dungeon level lead up to it and back to town.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-shot: after a punishing descent, the party climbs a stair into a cave beside a shady peddler's stand and must trade, recover and decide whether to go back down.
premise: Delvers worn down by the deep + an exit that opens beside a shady dealer = a chance to recover that comes with a price.

sensory.physical_environment: A cave near the spot where Wirt stands in Tristram, reached by stairs from the ninth level.
sensory.behaviors: Battered delvers emerge from the stairs and head toward the town and its peddler.
sensory.relationships: The cave joins the deep dungeon to Tristram and sits close to Wirt.
sensory.attitudes: Relief, wariness and a hint of bargaining with whoever waits at the cave mouth.
sensory.values: Survival, trade and the cost of coming back from the deep.

establishment.name: Tristram
establishment.worldview: The town needs its delvers alive and returning.
establishment.leverage: Rest, healing and goods at the top of the stairs.
establishment.flaw: Cannot reach or control what happens in the deep cave.

main_opponent.name: The dungeon's denizens
main_opponent.worldview: The deep levels belong to them, and the stair is a path out.
main_opponent.leverage: They can follow weakened delvers up the stairs.
main_opponent.flaw: They are drawn into the cave where delvers can ambush them.

thematic_shadow.name: Wirt
thematic_shadow.worldview: Everything has a price, including a safe return.
thematic_shadow.leverage: Stands right beside the way home and sells to those in need.
thematic_shadow.flaw: His wares and motives are never fully trusted.

tertiary_outcast.leverage: Has seen what lies below the ninth level.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: Exhausted and desperate, easy to exploit.

output_dial.level_1: The stair delivers the party to the cave and a calm, if shady, chance to trade and rest.
output_dial.level_2: The cave offers shelter but the party feels watched and bargains come at a cost.

output_dial.level_4: The cave becomes a breach that lets deep horrors spill toward Tristram while the party is spent.

threat_clocks.name: Deep Pursuit
