title: Diablo's Monster Templates
summary: The many monsters of the dungeon derive from a few general templates, the Undead, the Demons and the Animals. Added magical immunities or a distance attack modify each, so a new foe can be read as a variation on a known one.
standalone_fallback: Use it as a GM design tool. Pick a base template (Undead, Demon or Animal), add one twist such as a magical immunity or a ranged attack, and present the result as a new monster that veterans can half-recognize.
premise: A delver who trusts what they know about a monster type + a variant with a twist added = a lesson that must be partly relearned.

sensory.physical_environment: Dungeon halls and caverns populated by recognizable kinds of creature, each kind showing a family resemblance.
sensory.behaviors: Monsters behave according to their base type, with a twist added, such as a distance attack.
sensory.relationships: Many monsters are derivations of a general type, so variants are kin to their base template.
sensory.attitudes: Diverse on the surface, but a delver who knows the template can anticipate the foe.
sensory.values: Pattern recognition. Knowing the template is half of knowing the monster.

establishment.name: The Undead
establishment.worldview: The oldest and most orderly template, risen dead in ranks.
establishment.leverage: Numerous variants built on one base.
establishment.flaw: Predictable once the template is understood.

main_opponent.name: The Demons
main_opponent.worldview: A template of infernal predators who form the core threat.
main_opponent.leverage: Added magical immunities and distance attacks make variants dangerous.
main_opponent.flaw: Reliance on the twist leaves them exposed once it is identified.

thematic_shadow.name: The Animals
thematic_shadow.worldview: Natural beasts that follow instinct and are still modified by the dungeon.
thematic_shadow.leverage: Simple, direct threats that are easy to underestimate.
thematic_shadow.flaw: Lack the sophistication of the other templates.

tertiary_outcast.name: The unclassified variants
tertiary_outcast.worldview: Monsters whose added immunities or distance attacks blur the template they came from.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: Surprise, because they break expectations about their base type.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: They are still derivations, so the base template reveals their weakness.

output_dial.level_1: The party recognizes the template and handles the variant with little trouble.
output_dial.level_2: A familiar monster arrives with an unexpected twist, and the party must adjust its approach.
output_dial.level_3: Several variants with different immunities or ranged attacks arrive together, and the party's habits fail it.
output_dial.level_4: The party's assumptions about the template are badly wrong, and an unrecognized immunity leaves it without an answer.

threat_clocks.name: Assumptions Fail
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party treats a variant as its base template and ignores the added immunity or distance attack.

yields_resource: A working taxonomy the party can use to predict and counter new monsters, and a GM shorthand for building them.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: The guide sorts the diverse monsters into three basic classes, the Undead, the Demons and the Animals. Many are derivations of a general type, given added magical immunities, a distance attack, or similar changes.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Use it as a framing device at the start of a delve or whenever a new monster is introduced. It consumes the party's bestiary knowledge and feeds the other monster modules, including early patterns and depth progression. An arrival goes well when the party learns the template and probes for the twist. It goes badly when it assumes the variant behaves exactly like its base.

title: The Dungeon
summary: The dark subterranean realm beneath Tristram, home of the Servants of Darkness. Its dank rooms and hordes grow harder with depth and lead down to the Cavern levels.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-shot delve. The party descends from a threatened town into a godless abattoir of dank rooms and dark halls, faces escalating hordes and a few Uniques resistant to common magic, and tries to reach a goal and get back out.
premise: A hero who goes below to end a nightmare + a realm packed with hordes and resistant Uniques that grows worse with every level = a descent that costs more the deeper they push.

sensory.physical_environment: Dank rooms and dark halls beneath the town.
sensory.behaviors: Flesh-eating demons, rotting corpses and winged beasties lurch, swarm and flutter through the halls.
sensory.relationships: The Servants of Darkness dwell here, and Uniques lead or accompany hordes of minions. The town above is connected by the descent.
sensory.attitudes: Hostile and predatory, with nothing sacred about it.
sensory.values: Appetite, domination and the ruin of the living.

establishment.name: The Servants of Darkness
establishment.worldview: The dungeon is their realm, and intruders are meat.
establishment.leverage: Numbers, depth, and Unique monsters resistant or immune to common magic.
establishment.flaw: Their strength is spread across levels, so they meet intruders piecemeal.

main_opponent.name: The three heroes
main_opponent.worldview: The darkness under the town must be explored and broken.
main_opponent.leverage: They explore the dungeon, and they bring varied skills and the will to descend.
main_opponent.flaw: They are few, and the dungeon grows harsher with depth.

thematic_shadow.name: Tristram
thematic_shadow.worldview: The town above survives only if the dungeon stays below.
thematic_shadow.leverage: It is the link to the surface, where supplies and rest lie.
thematic_shadow.flaw: It depends entirely on the descenders and cannot protect itself.

tertiary_outcast.name: A delver who stayed too long below
tertiary_outcast.worldview: Down here the only rule is to survive the next room.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: Knows the layout of rooms and halls that others have not mapped.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: Worn down, suspicious and possibly marked by what lives here.

output_dial.level_1: Quiet, dank halls with stray monsters and the sense of being watched.
output_dial.level_2: Hordes of minions and a resistant Unique make each room a real fight.
output_dial.level_3: Packs and Uniques converge, common magic fails, and retreat to the surface is in doubt.
output_dial.level_4: The abattoir closes around the party, every hall is held, and only a few leave alive.

threat_clocks.name: Descent toll
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party presses deeper without resting or resupplying.

threat_clocks.name: The Unique stirs
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party makes noise or kills with magic that a resistant Unique shrugs off.

yields_resource: Treasure, knowledge of the Servants of Darkness, and progress toward ending the threat beneath the town.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: The dungeon is the godless abattoir under Tristram. It is the realm of the Servants of Darkness and a trial of attrition for anyone who descends. It holds minion hordes, Uniques that shrug off common magic, and the Cavern levels deeper within.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Use it as the main hub of an adventure, with the town above as the safe base and the Cavern levels as the deeper escalation. It consumes the party's supplies and resolve and feeds the town with news of what lies below. An arrival goes well when the party scouts, rests and chooses fights, and badly when they treat every level as routine and meet a resistant Unique unprepared.

title: Dungeon Beneath the Cathedral
summary: A dungeon reached by a stone stairway descending from the ruined church; the entry point into the game's 16 dungeon levels and their peripheral environments.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-shot descent. The party takes the stone stairway from a ruined church into darkness, where the scent of death surrounds them and monsters wait below.
premise: Heroes who must go beneath the ruined church + a dark stair into the scent of death = a descent where each level brings more monsters and more mayhem

sensory.physical_environment: A stone stairway inside the church plunges down into darkness to a dungeon beneath the ruined cathedral.
sensory.behaviors: Monsters and mayhem fill the depths. A huge list of foes waits below.
sensory.relationships: The dungeon connects upward to the ruined cathedral and downward to many levels with a random mix of peripheral environments.
sensory.attitudes: The darkness is oppressive and the place feels like a threshold with no return.
sensory.values: Descent is the way forward, and survival is earned one level at a time.

establishment.name: The ruined cathedral above
establishment.worldview: The church was the surface's last claim on the dark, and it has fallen.
establishment.leverage: Its stairway is the only known way down.
establishment.flaw: It is ruined and offers no protection to those who leave it.

main_opponent.name: The monsters of the dungeon
main_opponent.worldview: The depths belong to them, and intruders are prey.
main_opponent.leverage: A huge list of foes means there is always another threat.
main_opponent.flaw: They have no unity beyond hunger and are separated level from level.

thematic_shadow.name: The scent of death
thematic_shadow.worldview: Everything that goes down eventually joins the dead.
thematic_shadow.leverage: It unsettles every arrival and marks the place as a grave.
thematic_shadow.flaw: It warns of danger and so lets a prepared party plan.

tertiary_outcast.name: The lone descender
tertiary_outcast.worldview: A hero who goes in alone owes nothing to anyone and has nothing to lose.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: They can move quietly and take risks a group cannot.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: They have no support, and the dark favours the monsters.

output_dial.level_1: The stairway is a quiet descent, and the scent of death and the darkness are the only threats on the first steps.
output_dial.level_2: Monsters begin to appear in the passages below the stair, and the party fights as it descends.
output_dial.level_3: The foes grow thick and varied, peripheral environments show up unexpectedly, and the way back is uncertain.
output_dial.level_4: The depths close around the party, mayhem is everywhere, and retreat up the stair is cut off.

threat_clocks.name: The dark closes in
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party descends without rest, light or supplies, or ignores warning signs.

yields_resource: The party gains access to the whole descent, its levels and peripheral environments, and the chance to push deeper.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: A stone stairway inside the ruined church plunges down into darkness. At the bottom is a dungeon where the scent of death surrounds the hero. It is the entry point for the full descent, a long run of levels that also house a random mix of peripheral environments, with a huge list of foes.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place it directly below the ruined cathedral as the campaign's main threshold. It consumes the party's light, nerve and supplies, and it feeds every deeper site, quest and set piece. Arrival goes well when the party descends prepared and treats the scent of death as a warning. It goes badly when they rush in unprepared, meet the first monsters in the dark, and find the stair behind them is the only way out.

title: Dungeon Level Progression
summary: Monster types are ordered by dungeon depth. Hidden and Goat Demons appear mid-to-lower, Vipers lower, Overlords and Magma Demons deep, Horned Demons in the middle stretch, and Knights near the bottom.
standalone_fallback: Use it as a descent table. Each stage down brings a new class of foe, and the party can run it as a sequence of escalating zones, each introduced by its signature monster.
premise: A party that pushes deeper for greater rewards + a dungeon that fields worse monsters at each stage = a climb in danger that tests whether they are ready.

sensory.physical_environment: A dungeon that grows more infernal with depth, from mid-level halls through lower reaches to the deep levels near the bottom.
sensory.behaviors: Each depth is marked by its signature monsters, and the party meets progressively fiercer foes as it descends.
sensory.relationships: Hidden and Goat Demons hold the mid-to-lower levels, Vipers the lower levels, Overlords and Magma Demons the deep dungeon, and Knights the bottom.
sensory.attitudes: Horned Demons are first expected somewhere in the middle stretch, a warning that the dungeon is turning dangerous.
sensory.values: Depth equals danger, and each tier of monsters marks a threshold the party must be ready to cross.

establishment.name: Overlords
establishment.worldview: Deep-dungeon powers who rule the lower reaches.
establishment.leverage: Their position deep in the dungeon means the party must pass them to go further.
establishment.flaw: They are far from the surface, so any party that reaches them is already worn down.

main_opponent.name: Knights
main_opponent.worldview: The last guardians near the bottom of the dungeon.
main_opponent.leverage: They block the final stretch and hit hardest against a weakened party.
main_opponent.flaw: Reaching them means the party has already survived everything above.

thematic_shadow.name: Horned Demons
thematic_shadow.worldview: The first sign that the dungeon has turned truly infernal.
thematic_shadow.leverage: Their appearance marks the change from manageable to serious.
thematic_shadow.flaw: They are only a herald, and the worst is still to come.

tertiary_outcast.name: Hidden and Goat Demons, Vipers and Magma Demons
tertiary_outcast.worldview: Mid and lower foes, each tied to its own stretch of the descent.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: Specialized threats that punish a party unprepared for their depth.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: Bound to their stretch of the dungeon, they are avoidable by leaving it.

output_dial.level_1: The party descends with the gear and knowledge to meet each new monster class as it arrives.
output_dial.level_2: A new class of monster appears earlier than expected, and the party must adapt to the threshold.
output_dial.level_3: The party presses deeper than it is ready for and meets Vipers, Magma Demons or Overlords without answers.
output_dial.level_4: Knights and the deepest powers meet a party that has run out of resources, and retreat is no longer possible.

threat_clocks.name: Descent Outpaces Readiness
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party goes deeper without adapting to the new class of monsters.

threat_clocks.name: Cut Off From the Surface
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party commits to the deep levels without resupply or an escape route.

yields_resource: A clear threat ladder for pacing a delve, and the rewards that come with passing each threshold.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: The walkthrough orders monsters by depth. Hidden and Goat Demons are found on the mid-to-lower levels, Vipers on the lower levels, Overlords and Magma Demons deep in the dungeon, and Knights near the bottom. Horned Demons are first expected in the middle stretch between two of the earlier levels.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Use it as the backbone for pacing a multi-session dungeon crawl. It consumes the party's readiness and bestiary knowledge and feeds the monster-template and early-pattern modules, since each tier is a variation on known templates. An arrival goes well when the party treats each new monster class as a signal to reassess. It goes badly when it pushes on assuming the next level will resemble the last.

title: Dungeon Stairways Back to Tristram
summary: Hidden stairways deep in the dungeon lead back to town, saving the player a long walk and enabling quick trips topside to replenish health and mana.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a delve-and-retreat loop. The party pushes into dangerous depths, finds a stairway or portal back to a safe settlement, and uses short trips to recover and resupply before pushing deeper.
premise: An explorer who pushes too far + a long, dangerous way home = a choice between overextending and using the shortcuts to recover

sensory.physical_environment: Stairways deep in the dungeon open onto town: one emerges from the crypt in the graveyard, another into a cave near where Wirt stands, and in the catacombs the mausoleum opens to return to town.
sensory.behaviors: The player makes quick trips topside to replenish health and mana rather than walking back out.
sensory.relationships: The deep dungeon is linked to Tristram by these hidden routes.
sensory.attitudes: Caution is rewarded. The guide advises the player to overextend less.
sensory.values: Efficiency, recovery, and knowing the shortcuts.

establishment.name: Tristram, the home town
establishment.worldview: The town is the refuge and the dungeon should be a round trip.
establishment.leverage: It offers recovery and resupply to anyone who can reach it.
establishment.flaw: It cannot help those who are too deep or too proud to come back.

main_opponent.name: The long way out
main_opponent.worldview: The dungeon wants delvers worn down far from safety.
main_opponent.leverage: Distance and attrition punish those who push on without a retreat.
main_opponent.flaw: It is defeated by anyone who learns the shortcuts.

thematic_shadow.name: The fissure to hell
thematic_shadow.worldview: The same deep stairs that lead home can also open the way to something worse.
thematic_shadow.leverage: One up staircase opens a fissure behind Pepin's house through which the player can return to hell, so the shortcut has a dark twin.
thematic_shadow.flaw: The card's wording is brief, so the exact meaning of that route is left to the GM.

tertiary_outcast.name: The overextended delver
tertiary_outcast.worldview: One more room, one more fight, and then home.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: Boldness can earn quick rewards.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: They ignore the stairs and the portal until it is too late.

output_dial.level_1: A known stairway or portal makes a trip home a minor interruption.
output_dial.level_2: The party must find and reach the right stairway, and the trip is a real but manageable choice.
output_dial.level_3: The party is deep and depleted, the nearest shortcut is far, and they must decide whether to press on or retreat.
output_dial.level_4: Every route home is cut off or compromised, and the party must survive with whatever they have left.

threat_clocks.name: Overextension
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party pushes deeper without recovering or checking for a way home

yields_resource: Safe recovery, resupply, and a reliable loop between town and dungeon.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: Short of the stairs, Town Portal is the quickest route home. But stairways deep in the dungeon also open avenues back to Tristram. A mid-depth stair emerges from the crypt in the graveyard, a deeper one leads to a cave near where Wirt stands, and a still deeper up staircase opens a fissure behind Pepin's house. Once the party reaches the catacombs, the mausoleum opens to return to town. The advice is to overextend less and make quick trips topside to replenish health and mana.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place it at intervals in a multi-level dungeon, tied to the town hub. It consumes the party's supplies and fatigue and feeds them back as recovered resources and new information from town. Arrival goes well when the party discovers a stairway at the moment of greatest need and the loop feels earned. It goes badly if the shortcuts remove all tension, so vary their discovery, keep some hidden, and let the fissure route hint at danger.

title: Early Dungeon Monster Pattern
summary: The first dungeon levels pair Skeletons, Archers, Fallen Ones and Zombies so that their tactics teach the patterns of tougher foes later on. The party learns by reading speed and range and by choosing the order of attack.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-room tactics puzzle. A fast skittish pack, a middling rank of footsoldiers with a few ranged shooters behind them, and a slow heavy hitter that slips away all enter in one fight. The party wins by choosing the order in which to deal with them.
premise: A cautious delver who reads how each monster moves + a mixed pack that punishes the wrong order of attack = tactics learned the hard way, or a rout.

sensory.physical_environment: Narrow early dungeon rooms where the shooters can find a distance to fire from and the pack can close in. Fallen Ones hide from the Archers.
sensory.behaviors: Most monsters chase the party once it enters their room, even those with ranged attacks. Ranged monsters find the party, then set up at a distance to fire. Fallen Ones close the gap fastest, and Zombies lag behind.
sensory.relationships: Fallen Ones hide from the Archers. Skeletons are the footsoldiers, some with an Archer variation. Zombies are slower and may slip away to be hunted later.
sensory.attitudes: Fallen Ones are fast but merely bothersome. Skeletons are middle-of-the-road. Zombies are slow but can deal out serious damage.
sensory.values: Reading speed relative to the rest of the level matters most. Dealing with threats in the right order matters more than raw force.

establishment.name: Skeletons
establishment.worldview: Middle-of-the-road footsoldiers holding the line and chasing intruders.
establishment.leverage: Steady numbers, with Archer variants adding range.
establishment.flaw: Unremarkable, so they are dangerous mainly when the party ignores the order of attack.

main_opponent.name: Archers
main_opponent.worldview: Find the intruder, set up at a distance, and fire.
main_opponent.leverage: Ranged pressure that punishes a party caught in the open.
main_opponent.flaw: Exposed once cornered, and cornering them first is the recommended answer.

thematic_shadow.name: Fallen Ones
thematic_shadow.worldview: Fast but merely bothersome, they hide from the Archers and are first to close the gap.
thematic_shadow.leverage: Speed that forces the party to commit early.
thematic_shadow.flaw: Weak individually, so they are dealt with first.

tertiary_outcast.name: Zombies
tertiary_outcast.worldview: Slow and relentless, able to deal serious damage.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: Heavy blows against anyone who lets them close.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: Slowness lets them be escaped, and the party must double back for any that got away.

output_dial.level_1: The party reads the speeds correctly and clears the rooms in a sensible order with only minor scrapes.
output_dial.level_2: Shooters and footsoldiers arrive together, and the party must corner the Archers while the Skeletons press.
output_dial.level_3: The party misjudges the order, so the Fallen Ones swarm them while Archers pin them and a Zombie lumbers into the gap.
output_dial.level_4: The party is caught in the open between fast chasers, a firing line and a heavy hitter and is overrun before it can regroup.

threat_clocks.name: Pack Closes the Gap
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party ignores the speed differences or lets ranged monsters set up at a distance.

threat_clocks.name: Stragglers Return
threat_clocks.advances_when: A Zombie escapes and the party fails to double back for it.

yields_resource: The party learns reusable tactical patterns of speed, range and order of attack that transfer to tougher foes deeper down.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: The early dungeon teaches by example. Skeletons with an Archer variation, quick Fallen Ones and slow Zombies each model a tactic found in worse monsters later. The recommended order is Fallen Ones first, then the Skeleton footsoldiers (cornering Archers first if they appear), then back for any Zombies that escaped. The first thing to note on meeting a monster is its speed relative to the rest of the level.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place this in the first stretch of a delve or at the start of a campaign as a tutorial encounter. It consumes party positioning and scouting information, and it feeds the party's habits for deeper levels, including the Counselor-type monsters in the depths, which do not chase and are the exception. An arrival goes well when the party identifies speeds and sequences its targets. It goes badly when the party stands still in the open and lets the shooters set up.

title: The Fissure behind Pepin's House
summary: A fissure in the ground behind Pepin's house, opened by the up staircase on dungeon level 13, through which travelers can return to hell.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-shot: the party climbs a staircase out of the depths and finds a crack in the earth behind a healer's house in a quiet village. Beyond it lies a way back down to somewhere far worse. They must decide whether to use it, seal it, or guard it.
premise: Heroes who climb toward safety + a door to hell opening at the doorstep of home = a choice between pursuing the evil and protecting the village.

sensory.physical_environment: A fissure in the ground behind Pepin's house, in the village of Tristram, opened where the upward staircase from level 13 emerges.
sensory.behaviors: Villagers go about their business next door, while travelers approach the crack to go back to hell.
sensory.relationships: It is tied to Tristram by location, to the dungeon by the staircase, and to Hell as a two-way connection.
sensory.attitudes: Treated as the way back to hell: a route for those who mean to return, and a danger to those who live beside it.
sensory.values: Resolve and return over comfort; the village's calm rests beside a passage it cannot close.

establishment.name: Pepin
establishment.worldview: A healer whose house stands beside the fissure and who wants the village safe and ordinary.
establishment.leverage: Trusted standing in Tristram and healing aid for those who return from the depths.
establishment.flaw: Cannot close or guard a passage to hell by himself.

main_opponent.name: Powers of Hell
main_opponent.worldview: Hell's denizens regard the fissure as a path between their realm and the village above.
main_opponent.leverage: The passage links Hell to Tristram.
main_opponent.flaw: Their reach depends on a single fixed opening that can be watched.

thematic_shadow.name: The returning hero
thematic_shadow.worldview: Whoever descends again accepts that the fight must be carried to its source.
thematic_shadow.leverage: Direct access to Hell via the fissure.
thematic_shadow.flaw: Leaves the village, and any unfinished business above, behind.

tertiary_outcast.name: Frightened villager
tertiary_outcast.worldview: Believes the crack should be sealed or fled from, whatever it costs the heroes.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: Knows the village and can raise alarm or hinder travelers.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: Has no means to act against what comes through.

output_dial.level_1: The fissure sits quiet behind the house, noticed only by those who know what it is.
output_dial.level_2: Travelers use the opening to descend while villagers keep an uneasy distance and rumors spread.
output_dial.level_3: The village is fearful as the opening becomes contested ground, with watchers posted and tempers short.
output_dial.level_4: The passage becomes a gateway into Tristram itself, and the village is overrun or abandoned.

threat_clocks.name: The Village Notices
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party's comings and goings, or noise from the fissure, draw attention from Tristram's residents.

threat_clocks.name: Something Climbs Out
threat_clocks.advances_when: The fissure is left unguarded or the party delays making a decision about it.

yields_resource: A direct route to Hell, and a defensible choke point to watch or seal.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: Taking the up staircase on level 13 opens a fissure in the ground behind Pepin's house, and through it one can return to hell. The scene is a threshold: safety in the village on one side, the source of the evil on the other.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place it as the end of a dungeon climb or the start of a final descent. It consumes the party's arrival from the dungeon and feeds directly into Hell and Tristram. An arrival goes well when the party has prepared, has a clear intent for the passage, and keeps the village out of harm. It goes badly when they arrive wounded and undecided, or when the opening is left unwatched and the village pays.

title: Hell
summary: The deep realm reached through the fissure behind Pepin's house on dungeon level 13.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-shot: the party steps through a crack in the earth into a hostile infernal realm and must press on to confront its source. The card says little about the realm, so the GM supplies its geography and inhabitants.
premise: Heroes who return to finish what they started + an infernal realm that offers no safe ground = a climax where the cost of the pursuit is faced.

sensory.physical_environment: A deep realm beyond the fissure; the source states nothing more, so details are left to the GM.
sensory.behaviors: Travelers arrive by the fissure and are expected to press onward.
sensory.relationships: Linked in both directions with the fissure behind Pepin's house.
sensory.attitudes: Hostile and final; entering it means returning to where the evil began.
sensory.values: Endurance and resolve; there is no retreat except back through the same passage.

establishment.name: Rulers of Hell
establishment.worldview: The realm's ruling powers, unnamed on this card, hold the deep as their own.
establishment.leverage: Control of the realm the party enters.
establishment.flaw: Their dominion is entered through a single known passage.

main_opponent.name: The returning party
main_opponent.worldview: Those who descend intend to end the threat at its source.
main_opponent.leverage: Arrival through the fissure and the resolve to continue.
main_opponent.flaw: Isolated from the surface and from healing.

thematic_shadow.name: Fallen predecessors
thematic_shadow.worldview: Earlier travelers who went down and did not come back, a warning of the realm's cost.
thematic_shadow.leverage: Traces and cautionary example.
thematic_shadow.flaw: They have already failed.

tertiary_outcast.name: Hell's lesser denizen
tertiary_outcast.worldview: A creature of the deep with no loyalty to the powers above it, willing to bargain.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: Knowledge of the realm's paths.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: Unreliable and hunted by its own kind.

output_dial.level_1: The realm is a watchful, oppressive place, and the party passes while mostly unnoticed.
output_dial.level_2: Hell's denizens contest the party's advance and the way forward demands effort and sacrifice.
output_dial.level_3: The party is cut off from the fissure and forced deeper, with resources failing.
output_dial.level_4: The party is overwhelmed in the deep, and the way back is lost.

threat_clocks.name: The Way Back Closes
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party lingers, takes losses, or fails to secure the passage behind them.

yields_resource: Confrontation with the source of the evil and a conclusive end to the descent.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: Hell is the deep realm reached through the fissure behind Pepin's house on dungeon level 13. The card states only that the fissure lets the player return to hell, so everything else about the realm is the GM's to define.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Use it as the campaign's final stage. It consumes the party's arrival via the fissure and feeds the climax. An arrival goes well when the party has prepared and knows their purpose. It goes badly when they enter hurt, divided or unprepared. Because the source is sparse, the GM should treat the realm's contents as invented material.

title: Hell Levels
summary: The bottom of the dungeon, with large crowds of magical monsters, Succubi and Counselor-type monsters. There is room to run, so ranged attackers can keep their distance, and the best treasure and Diablo himself are here.
standalone_fallback: Run the Hell levels as a final-descent one-shot. The party fights through crowds of magical monsters in open spaces, survives the Succubi, and reaches Diablo for the climax, with a way back to town opening along the way.
premise: A party worn down by the descent + open ground full of magical monsters, with Diablo waiting at the bottom = the best reward costs the hardest fights.

sensory.physical_environment: The bottom of the dungeon, with enough open room for ranged attackers to run and keep their distance, so they are not easily drawn through doorways.
sensory.behaviors: Large crowds of magical monsters press in. Succubi chase, so there is no such thing as a short combat. The Counselor-type monsters stay in the depths and do not pursue.
sensory.relationships: Diablo holds the last level. The merchants in town begin to stock random Elixirs once the party descends.
sensory.attitudes: Relentless and hostile, and the toughest road for those who must close to melee.
sensory.values: The best treasure in the game is held in the last levels.

establishment.name: Diablo
establishment.worldview: The bottom of the dungeon is his seat, and everything above is under his shadow.
establishment.leverage: He holds the deepest level and the best treasure around him.
establishment.flaw: He is fixed at the bottom and the party can choose when to come for him.

main_opponent.name: The Succubi
main_opponent.worldview: They hunt the intruders and never let a fight end quickly.
main_opponent.leverage: They chase, and the open ground gives them room to harry the party.
main_opponent.flaw: They are drawn into pursuit, which can be used to pull them apart from the crowd.

thematic_shadow.name: The Counselor-type monsters
thematic_shadow.worldview: They hold their ground in the depths and do not chase.
thematic_shadow.leverage: They are magical, dangerous at range and found deep in hell.
thematic_shadow.flaw: They do not pursue, so the party can avoid or pick them off from outside their reach.

tertiary_outcast.name: The Warrior
tertiary_outcast.worldview: The adventurer who must close to melee finds no cover and no chokepoint here.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: Strength and toughness for the fights that cannot be avoided.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: The open ground and ranged magic make this the roughest road for them.

output_dial.level_1: The party moves through the Hell levels with careful use of distance and finds good treasure with manageable fights.
output_dial.level_2: Crowds of magical monsters keep pressing, and the Succubi turn every fight into a long chase.
output_dial.level_3: The party is swarmed on open ground, with no doorways to funnel enemies and supplies running low.
output_dial.level_4: The party is overwhelmed by crowds and Succubi in the open, cut off from retreat, and Diablo waits at the end.

threat_clocks.name: The Party's Supplies Run Out
threat_clocks.advances_when: Long fights with the Succubi and crowds drain healing and resources before the party reaches the last level.

threat_clocks.name: Diablo's Approach
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party descends deeper or delays, bringing the confrontation closer.

yields_resource: The best treasure in the game, the confrontation with Diablo, and another way back to the town level.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: The Hell levels are the final stretch of the dungeon, with large crowds of magical monsters in open ground. Distance attackers do well here since they are not easily drawn through doorways, while the Warrior has the roughest road. Succubi are the particular danger, and the last levels hold the best treasure and Diablo.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place this as the final act of a dungeon campaign. It consumes the party's accumulated resources and feeds the climax with Diablo. Reaching it opens another route to Tristram, and the town's merchants begin stocking random Elixirs. An arrival goes well when the party comes prepared, uses distance and open ground to their advantage, and retreats to town to resupply. It goes badly when they push on without supplies or force melee in the open.

title: The Bone King's Tomb
summary: Reached through an obvious passage in the dungeon, Leoric's Tomb is a small level where the cursed king summons skeletons to defend himself. Destroying him earns the Skeleton Crown.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-shot dungeon crawl. The party finds a passage into a royal tomb, fights through waves of skeletons the undead king keeps summoning, and destroys him to claim his crown.
premise: A hero who wants to end a curse + a king who raises bones faster than they can be broken = a race to destroy him before his horde is unstoppable.

sensory.physical_environment: A small, enclosed tomb reached by an obvious passage from the dungeon above. Cramped chambers where bones gather.
sensory.behaviors: The king summons skeletons continually, so the longer the fight runs, the more of them there are.
sensory.relationships: A summoner and his endless servants. The party stands between the king and the world above.
sensory.attitudes: Urgency: the advice is to put him out of business as quickly as possible.
sensory.values: Speed over caution, and finality over mercy.

establishment.name: King Leoric
establishment.worldview: A ruler in death as in life, commanding his bonemen in his own tomb.
establishment.leverage: The power to summon skeletons without end.
establishment.flaw: He is bound to his tomb and his cursed form, and his strength is spent if he is struck down quickly.

main_opponent.name: The summoned skeleton horde
main_opponent.worldview: Servants without will that exist to protect the king.
main_opponent.leverage: Numbers, which grow the longer the fight lasts.
main_opponent.flaw: They fall when the summoner falls, and they have no tactics.

thematic_shadow.name: The hero who becomes the new tomb-robber
thematic_shadow.worldview: Taking the crown from a grave is a profit that may carry a price.
thematic_shadow.leverage: The prize of the Skeleton Crown.
thematic_shadow.flaw: Greed can make a rescue into plunder.

tertiary_outcast.name: A wandering survivor or looter in the tomb
tertiary_outcast.worldview: The dead king's chambers are a place to scavenge while the fighting is elsewhere.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: Knowledge of side passages.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: They are easily caught between the king and the party.

output_dial.level_1: The party moves quickly through the tomb and the king falls before his skeletons can gather.
output_dial.level_2: Waves of skeletons are fought off steadily and the king is destroyed after a hard battle.
output_dial.level_3: The skeletons multiply faster than the party can clear them and retreat becomes a real option.
output_dial.level_4: An insurmountable horde of bonemen overwhelms the party and the king's curse spreads beyond the tomb.

threat_clocks.name: The Bone Horde Grows
threat_clocks.advances_when: The king is left alive and summons more skeletons while the party is distracted or slow.

yields_resource: The Skeleton Crown, the end of the king's curse, and removal of the undead horde's threat.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: Leoric's Tomb is a small level reached through an obvious passage. The king summons skeletons, and the advice is to put him out of business as quickly as possible lest he create an insurmountable horde of bonemen. Destroying him yields the Skeleton Crown.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place it a short way below a mid-depth dungeon level, as a compact set piece. It consumes the knowledge of the curse, ideally from the tavern plea, and feeds a reward item and a sense of closure. It goes well when the pressure of the growing horde pushes the party to act decisively. It goes badly if the party lingers, since time is what the king exploits.

title: King Leoric's Tomb
summary: A cramped tomb stuffed with Skeletons, with a small room of obvious treasure chests and a hidden antechamber. The hidden area opens only when every crucified Skeleton in the large room's corners has been destroyed.
standalone_fallback: Run the tomb as a one-room puzzle fight. The party must find and destroy every crucified Skeleton in the corners of the large room to open the hidden door, then face what is behind it for the better treasure.
premise: A party that wants the easy treasure + a hidden chamber that opens only after a thorough clearing = greed rewarded only by patience and violence.

sensory.physical_environment: Cramped quarters stuffed with Skeletons, a small room with treasure chests in plain view, and a large room with a long northern wall.
sensory.behaviors: Crucified Skeletons stand guard in the corners. When the last falls to the ground, a door opens in the middle of the long northern wall.
sensory.relationships: The tomb belongs to King Leoric, who is entombed here. The Skeletons serve him, even after death.
sensory.attitudes: Oppressive and watchful, with the sense that the obvious treasure is bait.
sensory.values: Guarded royal treasure and the reward for thoroughness.

establishment.name: King Leoric
establishment.worldview: The tomb is his domain, and what lies in it is his to guard.
establishment.leverage: He commands the Skeletons and holds the treasure in his tomb.
establishment.flaw: He is bound to the tomb and cannot leave it.

main_opponent.name: The Crucified Skeletons
main_opponent.worldview: They guard the hidden door and exist to keep the antechamber sealed.
main_opponent.leverage: They stand in the corners of the large room and keep the door shut while any of them remains.
main_opponent.flaw: They are fixed in place, and destroying all of them is what opens the door.

thematic_shadow.name: The treasure-hunting adventurer
thematic_shadow.worldview: Anything sealed away is there to be taken.
thematic_shadow.leverage: They can open the tomb by clearing it methodically.
thematic_shadow.flaw: Greed for the easy chests may lead them to miss the hidden reward or to walk into the foes behind it.

tertiary_outcast.name: The antechamber's foes
tertiary_outcast.worldview: They wait out of sight behind the hidden door, apart from the rest of the tomb.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: They hit a party that is already worn down by the Skeletons.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: They only act once the door is opened, so the party can prepare for them.

output_dial.level_1: The party quietly clears the Skeletons, opens the door and takes the treasure with little trouble.
output_dial.level_2: The cramped rooms make every fight messy, and the party must hunt down each crucified Skeleton before the door appears.
output_dial.level_3: The party enters the antechamber already worn out, and the foes inside press them hard in the tight space.
output_dial.level_4: The party is overwhelmed in the cramped tomb, trapped between the Skeletons and the antechamber's guardians, with the treasure out of reach.

threat_clocks.name: The Party Is Worn Down
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party fights the Skeletons in the cramped rooms without resting or retreating.

yields_resource: Treasure from the chests in the small room and better treasure from the hidden antechamber.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: The tomb tests thoroughness. Obvious treasure chests wait in the small room, but the real prize lies behind a door that appears only after every crucified Skeleton in the large room's corners is destroyed. Inside are more foes and more treasure.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place this tomb partway down the dungeon, as a mid-game side objective reached from an early level. It consumes the party's combat strength and feeds loot back toward town. It links to the scene of opening the secret antechamber. An arrival goes well when the party scouts the corners and clears them methodically. It goes badly when they take the obvious chests, miss the hidden door, or go in wounded.

title: Level 2 Cathedral
summary: A desecrated cathedral on the second dungeon level where the Butcher's first quest begins, with a dying townsman at the church entrance.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-shot. The party reaches a profaned cathedral, meets a dying townsman at its door, and takes up his plea to deal with the horror inside.
premise: Heroes who answer a dying plea + a sanctuary turned into a slaughterhouse = a quest that proves what the dungeon does to the innocent.

sensory.physical_environment: A desecrated cathedral, with a church entrance where a townsman lies dying.
sensory.behaviors: The dying townsman gasps out warnings. Arriving heroes hurry inside, torn between aiding him and pressing on.
sensory.relationships: The townsman stands for the townsfolk who depend on the heroes. The Butcher is the quest's implied source of dread.
sensory.attitudes: Dread, urgency, and horror at profanation.
sensory.values: Duty to the helpless, and the sanctity that has been violated.

establishment.name: The townsfolk
establishment.worldview: Someone must cleanse the church so the community can survive.
establishment.leverage: Desperate need, and the heroes' conscience.
establishment.flaw: They can only send those who may not come back.

main_opponent.name: The Butcher
main_opponent.worldview: The cathedral is his domain to defile.
main_opponent.leverage: He claims the ground and the terror it inspires.
main_opponent.flaw: He is one fixed horror, and the quest centers on beating him.

thematic_shadow.name: The dying townsman
thematic_shadow.worldview: A last warning matters more than his own life.
thematic_shadow.leverage: He is the first witness to what happened.
thematic_shadow.flaw: He is fading, and what he knows may die with him.

tertiary_outcast.name: The faithful who fled
tertiary_outcast.worldview: The church is lost and must be abandoned.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: They know the cathedral's former shape.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: Their fear leaves them useless for the fight.

output_dial.level_1: The party finds the cathedral defiled and takes the townsman's last words as a grim hook.
output_dial.level_2: The desecration is plain, the quest begins in earnest, and the party moves inside carefully.
output_dial.level_3: Signs of the Butcher's work close in, the cathedral turns into a gauntlet, and retreat is costly.
output_dial.level_4: The party is overwhelmed in the defiled sanctuary, and the dying townsman's fate becomes theirs.

threat_clocks.name: The Townsman Fades
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party delays at the entrance or ignores what the townsman tells them.

threat_clocks.name: The Desecration Deepens
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party fails to press the quest or retreats from the cathedral.

yields_resource: The start of the Butcher quest, with the townsman's warning and the chance to restore the church.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: The cathedral is where the Butcher's first quest begins. Its two canon images are a desecrated sanctuary and a dying townsman at the entrance. Use them to make the stakes personal before any fight starts. How the Butcher behaves and what the party finds inside are GM judgements.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place it early in the second dungeon level, as the first major hook after the party has descended from the surface. It consumes a party ready for combat and feeds the Butcher quest and evidence of desecration. It goes well when the party honors the dying plea and enters prepared. It goes badly when they rush in, or leave the townsman to die without learning what he knew.

title: Magical item prefixes and suffixes
summary: Magical weapons, armor, amulets and cloaks gain randomly assigned prefixes and suffixes that define their properties. Items with both a positive prefix and suffix are best, and prefixes can modify damage, armor, accuracy, Mana, resistances and spell levels.
standalone_fallback: Run it as an item-appraisal scene: the party finds a magical item and learns its random properties from its prefix and suffix. They decide whether to keep, trade or fear what it does.
premise: Adventurers who crave a better edge + loot whose properties are assigned by chance = they gamble on what each find is truly worth.

sensory.physical_environment: A weapon, armor, amulet or cloak whose name carries a prefix and suffix that hint at what it holds.
sensory.behaviors: Characters read an item's name, compare its properties, and weigh keeping or trading it.
sensory.relationships: Each item's prefix and suffix together define it, so the pairing matters as much as either part.
sensory.attitudes: Excitement at a lucky roll and wariness that a bad suffix or prefix may curse the find.
sensory.values: Items with both a prefix and a suffix, if positive, are best.

establishment.name: The item's makers or the roll of chance
establishment.worldview: Properties are assigned at random and define an item's worth.
establishment.leverage: Prefixes and suffixes grant resistances, damage, armor, To Hit and Mana bonuses, and spell-level boosts.
establishment.flaw: Outcomes are unpredictable and some properties may be negative.

main_opponent.name: The unlucky finder
main_opponent.worldview: Every find should be a prize, so bad rolls feel like betrayal.
main_opponent.leverage: They can discard or trade a weak item.
main_opponent.flaw: They cannot control what properties an item receives.

thematic_shadow.name: The collector
thematic_shadow.worldview: Only items with both a good prefix and a good suffix are worth keeping.
thematic_shadow.leverage: Discernment and patience.
thematic_shadow.flaw: Obsession with the best may leave them without a workable tool.

tertiary_outcast.name: The class who can't use it
tertiary_outcast.worldview: A role that cannot use a property sees it as worthless trade goods.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: They can sell or trade it.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: They miss what the item might have done in other hands.

output_dial.level_1: The party finds a modestly enchanted item that gives a small, welcome edge.
output_dial.level_2: A well-matched prefix and suffix make an item clearly useful and spark trading or debate over who should hold it.
output_dial.level_3: A mismatched or negative property makes the item risky, and the party must decide whether to rely on it.
output_dial.level_4: A powerful but flawed item grants vast advantage at a terrible cost, tempting the party into a disastrous bargain.

threat_clocks.name: The Gamble Sours
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party relies on an unidentified or poorly matched item without checking its properties.

yields_resource: Knowledge of an item's properties and a useful, well-matched magical item.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: When a character acquires a magical weapon, armor, amulet or cloak, a set of randomly assigned prefixes and suffixes defines its properties. Prefixes modify things such as damage, armor, To Hit, Mana, resistances and spell levels. Items with both a prefix and a suffix, if positive, are best. The source gives only partial prefix tables.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place this wherever the party gains loot, such as the reward from a slain Unique. It consumes unidentified items and feeds the party's capabilities and trading choices. An arrival goes well when the party reads the name, matches the item to its wielder, and gains a clear boost. It goes badly when they assume any magical item is good, equip a negative property, or give a prize to a character who cannot use it.

title: Magical Resistance
summary: Three kinds of magic resistance, General, Fire and Lightning, protect the hero from magical attacks. Because magic does not wear down armor the way physical blows do, resistance can justify wearing otherwise weak armor.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a single encounter against casters, such as succubi, where the party must decide whether to trade solid armor for protection against magic, and see how their choice plays out.
premise: Heroes who armor themselves against blades + enemies who attack with magic instead = a gamble over which protection to wear.

sensory.physical_environment: Armor and gear marked by what they guard against, with magical blasts of fire and lightning striking them.
sensory.behaviors: Heroes weigh equipment, trading physical protection for resistance against magic.
sensory.relationships: Casting monsters like the Succubi press against heroes who prepare for their attacks.
sensory.attitudes: Wariness of magic, and willingness to wear weak armor if it shields against spells.
sensory.values: Preparedness and the right protection for the right threat.

establishment.name: The hero's equipment
establishment.worldview: Resistance is a deliberate defensive choice among three types: General, Fire and Lightning.
establishment.leverage: It blunts magical attacks that armor cannot stop.
establishment.flaw: Gear chosen for resistance may be weak against physical blows.

main_opponent.name: The Succubi
main_opponent.worldview: Magic is a weapon that bypasses ordinary armor.
main_opponent.leverage: Their magical attacks are not stopped by physical protection, though they leave armor Durability intact.
main_opponent.flaw: General magic resistance is aimed squarely at monsters like them.

thematic_shadow.name: Physical armor
thematic_shadow.worldview: Sturdy plate is the answer to every threat.
thematic_shadow.leverage: Strong against physical attacks.
thematic_shadow.flaw: It wears down under physical attacks and does nothing special against magic.

tertiary_outcast.name: The hero in weak but warded gear
tertiary_outcast.worldview: Magical protection is worth more than solid armor.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: Strong resistance to the magic that threatens them.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: Exposed to physical attack.

output_dial.level_1: A hero's resistance shrugs off a stray spell and the fight carries on.
output_dial.level_2: Magical attackers pressure the party, and those with the right resistance hold the line while others struggle.
output_dial.level_3: Fire and lightning assaults overwhelm unprepared heroes, and the party must rethink its gear.
output_dial.level_4: Magic strikes with no matching resistance, leaving the party stripped of defenses and in flight.

threat_clocks.name: Unwarded Against Magic
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party meets magical attackers without matching resistance.

yields_resource: Resistance to General, Fire or Lightning magic, and the knowledge that warded gear can be worth wearing even when its physical protection is weak.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: Magic Resistance comes in three types: General, which concerns monsters like the Succubi, and then Fire and Lightning. Magical attacks do not damage armor Durability as physical attacks do, so resistance can justify wearing otherwise weak armor. Which type to prepare for is the central decision.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place before a magic-heavy area or boss and let the party learn what they face beforehand, so the choice is informed. It consumes the party's gear options and feeds the Character Class Philosophy theme of secondary configurations, since resistance is part of a flexible build. Arrival goes well if the party scouts and prepares the right ward. It goes badly if they arrive in heavy armor with no resistance and meet fire, lightning or the Succubi unprepared.

title: Magical Shrines
summary: Shrines trigger when stepped upon and give only a cryptic message. Their effects range from helpful to costly, so every one is a gamble that rewards preparation.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a single chamber holding one unmarked shrine. The party must decide whether to activate it after reading an ambiguous message, with the outcome a blessing, a trade-off or a hidden cost.
premise: An adventurer eager for a boon + a shrine that speaks only in riddles = a blind gamble on power at a possible price.

sensory.physical_environment: Lone shrines scattered through the dungeon, each of which activates when you step up to it.
sensory.behaviors: Weary adventurers step up, read a cryptic message and then decide whether to risk the effect, often missing the hint.
sensory.relationships: The shrine and the one who approaches it, with no guide except the message itself.
sensory.attitudes: The hint is often lost on the weary adventurer, so shrines breed both hope and suspicion.
sensory.values: Knowledge, readiness and a willingness to gamble on uncertain power.

establishment.name: The shrine's makers
establishment.worldview: Power is offered in riddles to those who deserve it.
establishment.leverage: A dungeon dotted with boons that lure explorers onward.
establishment.flaw: Their messages are so cryptic that few can use them.

main_opponent.name: The tainted shrine
main_opponent.worldview: Every gift has a hidden price.
main_opponent.leverage: Costly trade-offs that punish the rash, such as lost mana or weakened gear.
main_opponent.flaw: Its cost is only a gamble, and careful players can avoid it.

thematic_shadow.name: The reckless seeker
thematic_shadow.worldview: Any boon is worth the risk, so activate everything.
thematic_shadow.leverage: Quick access to power the cautious never reach.
thematic_shadow.flaw: Unprepared, they pay full price for effects they cannot use.

tertiary_outcast.name: The weary wanderer
tertiary_outcast.worldview: The hints mean nothing and one should simply press on.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: Speed and economy of effort.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: Misses the shrines that clearly reward preparation.

output_dial.level_1: A shrine grants a small, welcome boon and the party moves on slightly stronger.
output_dial.level_2: A shrine's message is unclear and its effect is a mixed trade, giving something and taking something else.
output_dial.level_3: A badly timed shrine exacts a real cost, such as gear turned brittle or a spell upgrade bought with lost mana.
output_dial.level_4: The party stumbles on a shrine whose effect spoils the whole expedition, leaving their kit damaged and their plan in ruins.

threat_clocks.name: Gamble turns sour
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party activates shrines without reading the message or preparing for its effect.

yields_resource: A boon such as improved attributes, sturdier items, a spell upgrade or a protective shield, along with knowledge of what each shrine does.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: Most of the time a shrine offers only a cryptic clue to its function, and the hint is often lost on the weary adventurer. The guide catalogues shrine types, their messages and effects, which cover stat changes, durability, spell upgrades, mana shields, chest regeneration, potion transforms, a level teleport and level-wide mapping or identification. Some, such as the Cryptic, Thaumaturgic and Spiritual shrines, clearly reward preparation before activating.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Use shrines as small side rooms or optional detours inside any dungeon floor. They consume the party's caution and sometimes their mana or gear condition, and they feed boons into later fights. An arrival goes well when the party reads the message, prepares and weighs the trade; it goes badly when they press blindly and pay for effects they did not want.
