figures.value: Holy Bolt level +2, lose 1/10 max Mana

title: Narrow Path Between Lava Lakes
summary: A crossing between two lava lakes in the cave-like midlevels, narrower than a doorway and likely the most restrictive hurdle a horde of monsters can meet. Defenders gain the advantage; attackers must funnel through.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-room set piece: a hero or party holds a crossing between lava lakes while a horde tries to funnel through, and the fight turns on who controls the choke.
premise: A fighter who holds the line + a path too narrow for a horde = a stand where numbers stop mattering and preparation decides the day.

sensory.physical_environment: A narrow path between two lava lakes, narrower than even a doorway, in the cave-like midlevels.
sensory.behaviors: Brutes slow to form a single-file line; a strong character stands toe-to-toe with one or two foes while rogues rain arrows on the crossing.
sensory.relationships: Defenders at the crossing against a horde trying to organize on the far side.
sensory.attitudes: Grim confidence among defenders, frustration among the bunched horde.
sensory.values: Position, discipline and picking enemies off while they organize.

establishment.name: The strong character holding the crossing
establishment.worldview: One steady fighter at the choke is worth a dozen in the open.
establishment.leverage: Can stand toe-to-toe with one or two foes at a time.
establishment.flaw: Cannot hold forever alone and is exposed to anything that goes around or over.

main_opponent.name: The horde of monsters
main_opponent.worldview: Weight of numbers will break any line.
main_opponent.leverage: Sheer numbers and persistence.
main_opponent.flaw: Slow to form a single-file line, which makes them easy to pick off.

thematic_shadow.name: Poison Spitters
thematic_shadow.worldview: Range makes the choke irrelevant.
thematic_shadow.leverage: They attack from a distance, though lava lakes slightly inhibit their movement.
thematic_shadow.flaw: Hampered by the lava around them.

tertiary_outcast.name: The rogue archers
tertiary_outcast.worldview: Stay back, shoot the crossing, never be caught in the melee.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: A hail of arrows on the crossing while the brutes organize.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: Fragile if the line breaks.

output_dial.level_1: The crossing is held easily; the horde trickles through the narrow path and is picked off.
output_dial.level_2: The line holds with effort as the defender trades blows with a pair of foes while archers thin the rest.
output_dial.level_3: Ranged attackers and sheer pressure strain the defenders, and the crossing begins to fail.
output_dial.level_4: The line breaks, and the party is overrun at the lava's edge with no room to retreat.

threat_clocks.name: The Line Cracks
threat_clocks.advances_when: The defender is worn down, ranged enemies find targets, or the archers lose their cover.

yields_resource: A defensible position that neutralizes a horde's numbers, and time to thin it out.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: A narrow path between two lava lakes, common in the cave-like midlevels, is narrower than even a doorway and probably the most restrictive hurdle a horde of monsters can run into. It turns a numbers fight into a positional one: a strong character can stand toe-to-toe with one or two foes, and rogues can hit the crossing with arrows while the brutes slowly form a single-file line.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place it in the cave-like midlevels, within the Cavern levels to which it is tied. It consumes the party's preparation and ranged support and feeds their ability to survive a horde. It pairs with the Caves and with a restorative stop such as the Blood Fountain afterward. An arrival goes well when the party sets a defender at the choke and archers behind. It goes badly when they are caught on the wrong side, lack ranged support, or face Poison Spitters, which lava only slightly slows. Whether the lava itself threatens those standing by it is not stated on the card and is the GM's call.

title: Ogden's Sign Quest
summary: Demons have stolen the sign of Ogden's Rising Sun Inn and Tavern. Snotspill will not let the party descend until it is recovered, and then a choice awaits about who gets it.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-shot where a tavern's stolen sign sits in a monster's lair. A gatekeeper blocks the stairs until the sign is claimed, and the party must decide between giving it to the gatekeeper or returning it to its owner.
premise: A party that wants to go deeper + a gatekeeper who blocks the stairs until a stolen sign is returned = a choice between a quick payoff and an honest reward.

sensory.physical_environment: The fourth dungeon level, Snotspill's set piece, and the staircase down to the fifth level.
sensory.behaviors: Adventurers hunt for the sign, deal with Snotspill and decide what to do with it afterward.
sensory.relationships: Ogden the Tavern Owner gives the quest, Snotspill blocks the stairs, and Cain and Adria offer advice.
sensory.attitudes: Ogden wants his sign back, and the little creature Snotspill treats the stairs as his to guard.
sensory.values: Fair dealing, a tavern's pride, and the pull of a quick reward.

establishment.name: Ogden the Tavern Owner
establishment.worldview: A sign is a tavern's name and a town's small piece of normal life.
establishment.leverage: He gives the quest and, if the sign is returned to him, produces the Harlequin Crest.
establishment.flaw: He cannot retrieve the sign himself.

main_opponent.name: Snotspill
main_opponent.worldview: The stairs are his to control, and nobody passes without the sign.
main_opponent.leverage: He blocks the way down to the fifth level until the sign is claimed.
main_opponent.flaw: He can be handed the sign and then killed for a random item.

thematic_shadow.name: The demons who stole the sign
thematic_shadow.worldview: Even a humble tavern sign is a trophy worth taking from the living.
thematic_shadow.leverage: They hold the town's small pride to ransom in the depths.
thematic_shadow.flaw: Their theft draws the very heroes who will undo it.

tertiary_outcast.name: Cain the Storyteller and Adria the Witch
tertiary_outcast.worldview: Counsel is cheap and the choices belong to others.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: They advise on the quest and its options.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: They cannot make the choice for the party.

output_dial.level_1: The sign is found, the stairs open and the party returns or hands it over without complication.
output_dial.level_2: The party must weigh the two options carefully, with Ogden's gratitude on one side and a random item on the other.
output_dial.level_3: The party hesitates over the choice while Snotspill still blocks the stairs, stalling their descent.
output_dial.level_4: The sign is lost or mishandled, the way down remains shut, and the town's goodwill sours.

threat_clocks.name: Stairs stay shut
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party fails to find the sign or delays the choice while Snotspill continues to block the way.

yields_resource: Passage down to the fifth level, and either the Harlequin Crest from Ogden or a random item from Snotspill.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: Those demons have stolen the sign to Ogden’s Rising Sun Inn and Tavern, and it's up to you to get it back. The party must claim the sign before Snotspill will let them advance from the fourth to the fifth level. After recovery there are two options: hand it to Snotspill, who is then killed for a random item, or return it to Ogden, who produces the Harlequin Crest.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place this on the fourth dungeon level, tied to Snotspill's set piece and the staircase beyond. It consumes the party's time and the goodwill of Ogden, and it feeds the descent into deeper levels. An arrival goes well when the party gets the sign and chooses knowingly between the reward from Ogden and the item from Snotspill; it goes badly when they stall or lose the sign and find the stairs still shut.

title: Opening Arrival in the Village
summary: The hero arrives in a somber, twilit village, hears of dark riders and rituals at a ruined cathedral, passes a dying man at the church entrance, and faces a stone stairway leading down into darkness.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-shot prologue. The party arrives in a dimming village, gathers rumors from a frightened few, sees the dying man at the church door, and chooses whether to descend the stairs. The descent is the cliffhanger.
premise: A newcomer who cannot ignore suffering + a village too frightened to explain its own doom = a descent into the dark with half the story missing

sensory.physical_environment: A somber, twilit village. Dim light seeps from the church doorway and a stone stairway plunges into darkness.
sensory.behaviors: The anxious, dwindling populace talks in hushed fragments. A dying man writhes at the church entrance.
sensory.relationships: The villagers are strangers who now lean on the newcomer. They are cut off from one another by fear and loss.
sensory.attitudes: Dread, resignation and a thin hope that someone will do something about the cathedral.
sensory.values: Survival, the memory of a safer village, and the faint expectation that outsiders can still help.

establishment.name: The dwindling villagers
establishment.worldview: The village is dying and an outsider might be its last chance.
establishment.leverage: They hold the rumors and local knowledge the hero needs to begin.
establishment.flaw: Fear keeps them vague, so their information is incomplete and secondhand.

main_opponent.name: The dark riders and the cathedral ritualists
main_opponent.worldview: The village is prey and the ruined cathedral is a gate to be used.
main_opponent.leverage: Their invasion has already thinned the population and set the village's fear.
main_opponent.flaw: Their nature and purpose are unclear, so they are known only through rumor and consequences.

thematic_shadow.name: The dying man at the church entrance
thematic_shadow.worldview: Suffering has already come to this door, and the descent will cost more of the same.
thematic_shadow.leverage: He is a visible, immediate proof of the stakes.
thematic_shadow.flaw: He cannot speak or act in any lasting way, and may be a warning rather than a guide.

tertiary_outcast.name: A villager who has stopped hoping
tertiary_outcast.worldview: Nothing can be done and newcomers merely die in the dark.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: They can discourage or mislead the party with despair.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: Their resignation leaves them with no plan and no allies.

output_dial.level_1: The village is quiet and tense, rumors come freely, and the stairway is just an ominous option.
output_dial.level_2: Villagers speak urgently about riders and rituals, and the dying man makes the cost of delay plain.
output_dial.level_3: More villagers have vanished or fled, the church doorway pulses with unnatural light, and the party feels the descent is overdue.
output_dial.level_4: The village is nearly empty, the riders are close, and the stairway is the only place left that offers any answers.

threat_clocks.name: The village empties
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party delays, dithers, or ignores the villagers' fears

yields_resource: Rumors, motivation and a clear route into the dungeon. The party leaves with their first leads and a reason to care.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: This is the opening beat. A newcomer enters a village already losing its people to dark riders and strange rituals at a ruined cathedral. A dying man at the church entrance and a stairway descending into darkness make the choice plain: go down or turn away.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place it at the very start of a campaign or one-shot, with the dungeon directly beneath. It feeds the rumor clue about riders and rituals and gives the party a reason to return to town later. It consumes only the party's willingness to engage. Arrival goes well when the party gets a sense of place, a cause worth fighting for, and one or two leads. It goes badly if the GM lectures instead of letting the villagers be anxious and incomplete, or if the party treats the dying man as scenery.

title: Opening the Secret Antechamber of King Leoric's Tomb
summary: In the large room of King Leoric's Tomb, the player destroys every crucified Skeleton in the corners. When the last one falls, a door opens in the middle of the long northern wall and reveals a secret antechamber with more foes and treasures.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-room puzzle fight. The party enters a chamber with a crucified Skeleton in each corner, learns that destroying them all opens a hidden door in the northern wall, and then faces the guardians and loot behind it.
premise: Adventurers who clear every last foe + a tomb that rewards thoroughness with a hidden door = treasure and danger beyond what they expected

sensory.physical_environment: A large tomb room with a crucified Skeleton in each corner and a long northern wall that conceals a door.
sensory.behaviors: The party hunts down each corner Skeleton, tracks which are still standing, and listens for the stone to move.
sensory.relationships: The Skeletons, the hidden door and the antechamber are tied together as a lock and its key.
sensory.attitudes: The room seems finished until the last Skeleton falls, and then it turns out to have been waiting.
sensory.values: Thoroughness is rewarded, and anything left undone keeps the secret shut.

establishment.name: The tomb's builders
establishment.worldview: What lies in the tomb should be guarded and found only by the thorough.
establishment.leverage: The hidden door and its guardians.
establishment.flaw: A lock that depends on a visible rule can be solved by anyone who notices the rule.

main_opponent.name: The antechamber's foes
main_opponent.worldview: Intruders who open the door have come for what the tomb protects.
main_opponent.leverage: They lie in wait behind the opened door, with the party's attention spent on the corners.
main_opponent.flaw: They guard the treasure but cannot stop the door from opening.

thematic_shadow.name: The crucified Skeletons
thematic_shadow.worldview: They exist to hold the door shut by their very presence.
thematic_shadow.leverage: Each one is a link in the lock, so the party must deal with all of them.
thematic_shadow.flaw: Destroying them is the very act that opens the door.

tertiary_outcast.name: The scavenger who skips the corners
tertiary_outcast.worldview: The main path is enough, and side duties are a waste of time.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: A faster route through the tomb.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: They never find the secret antechamber, or find it only after others have emptied it.

output_dial.level_1: The last Skeleton falls, the door slides open, and a small band of foes and a modest cache wait behind it.
output_dial.level_2: The door opens onto a proper antechamber with a tougher group of foes and worthwhile treasure.
output_dial.level_3: The party is already worn down when the door opens, and the guardians behind it strike before they can regroup.
output_dial.level_4: The opened door releases a force that overwhelms the weakened party and turns the antechamber into a trap.

threat_clocks.name: The Antechamber Stirs
threat_clocks.advances_when: Each corner Skeleton is destroyed, or the party makes enough noise that the guardians behind the wall are alerted.

yields_resource: Antechamber treasure, plus the satisfaction and advantage of having solved the room's lock.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: In the large room of King Leoric's Tomb, a crucified Skeleton stands in each corner. Destroying all of them opens a door in the middle of the long northern wall. Behind it lies a secret antechamber with more foes and treasures. The puzzle rewards a party that clears the room completely instead of passing through.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place it in the large room of King Leoric's Tomb, as a side objective that sits beside the main route. It consumes the party's attention and resources in the corner fights and feeds treasure and a harder encounter beyond the door. An arrival goes well when the GM signals the Skeletons as a pattern, lets the party discover the door, and sets the antechamber's difficulty against what they have spent. It goes badly if the trigger is unclear, if a missed Skeleton blocks progress with no hint, or if the reward does not justify the risk.

title: Poison Water Quest Battle
summary: During the Poison Water Quest, the Fallen Ones and a Goat Demon band together and attack the party at once.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-shot: while the party seeks to cleanse a poisoned water source, a band of Fallen Ones and a Goat Demon close in from different sides and fight as one force.
premise: A party pursuing a quest + enemies of different kinds who gang up = a hard fight that forces focus and coordination.

sensory.physical_environment: The setting of the Poison Water Quest, with foes closing in.
sensory.behaviors: The Fallen Ones and the Goat Demon gang up on the party together.
sensory.relationships: Normally separate monsters fighting in concert against the party.
sensory.attitudes: Aggressive, converging hostility.
sensory.values: Overwhelm the intruder through numbers and combined force.

establishment.name: The party's quest-giver
establishment.worldview: The poisoned water must be dealt with.
establishment.leverage: Directs the party and offers reward.
establishment.flaw: Sends the party into danger it cannot fully see.

main_opponent.name: The Goat Demons
main_opponent.worldview: Strength to be wielded with their allies against intruders.
main_opponent.leverage: Heavy force that backs up the Fallen Ones.
main_opponent.flaw: Dependent on coordination with the Fallen Ones.

thematic_shadow.name: The Fallen Ones
thematic_shadow.worldview: Swarm and overwhelm.
thematic_shadow.leverage: Numbers and flanking.
thematic_shadow.flaw: Weakened once the group is split or the Goat Demon falls.

tertiary_outcast.name: A party member caught alone
tertiary_outcast.worldview: Survival comes first.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: Can draw enemy attention away.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: Isolated and exposed when the enemies gang up.

output_dial.level_1: The party anticipates the ambush, holds a good position, and fights the group piece by piece.
output_dial.level_2: The enemies hit together and the party must fight hard and use terrain to avoid being overwhelmed.
output_dial.level_3: The party is surrounded by the combined force and forced to retreat or split up while the quest is endangered.
output_dial.level_4: The combined assault breaks the party, leaving them routed and the quest in jeopardy.

threat_clocks.name: Closing Pincer
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party fails to separate the Fallen Ones from the Goat Demon, or lingers in the open.

yields_resource: Quest progress: surviving the battle clears the way to complete the Poison Water Quest.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: The card states that the Fallen Ones and the Goat Demon will gang up on the player during the Poison Water Quest. The situation is a combined-arms fight where two monster types act as one.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place it at a key point of the Poison Water Quest, such as approaching the objective. It consumes the party's resources and feeds quest completion. It goes well when the party divides the enemies or prepares a defensible position; it goes badly when they are caught in the open. Beyond the participants, the card gives no detail, so layout and numbers are the GM's judgement.

title: Poisoned Water Caverns
summary: A set-piece cavern level beyond a crack in the Level 2 wall, where a fouled underground spring is tainted by a demon infestation.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-shot cavern crawl. The party finds a crack in a wall marked 'To A Dark Passage', is ambushed by fallen ones on arrival, and fights through rock corridors of Goat Demons and lesser beasts to the fouled spring. They can cleanse it or flee.
premise: Heroes who follow every sign of hidden lore + a spring tainted by demons below = a fight through foul rock corridors to purify the water or be swallowed by the infestation

sensory.physical_environment: Rock corridors and caverns with a fouled waterway running through them, reached through a crack in the wall.
sensory.behaviors: Fallen ones wait at the arrival point. Goat Demons and lesser beasts hold the corridors.
sensory.relationships: The demon infestation has taken over a spring that once ran clean. Beasts follow the demons' lead.
sensory.attitudes: The place feels hidden and deliberately set apart. The ornate marking promises lore but delivers an ambush.
sensory.values: Taint is territory. Whoever holds the water holds the dark passage.

establishment.name: Fallen Ones
establishment.worldview: The cavern is theirs to guard, and arrivals are intruders to be met at the door.
establishment.leverage: They wait at the entry and so have the first strike on anyone who comes through.
establishment.flaw: They are posted to the arrival point and give ground once the party is past them.

main_opponent.name: Goat Demons
main_opponent.worldview: The caverns are a demon holding and the poisoned spring is proof of their claim.
main_opponent.leverage: They are heavier hitters than the lesser beasts and are spread through the corridors.
main_opponent.flaw: They are bound to the corridors and are drawn out piecemeal.

thematic_shadow.name: The marked wall
thematic_shadow.worldview: Treasure and truth are hidden behind ornament, and curiosity is the way in.
thematic_shadow.leverage: The 'To A Dark Passage' label draws in anyone who loves lore.
thematic_shadow.flaw: The ornament promises an answer it does not give, and the reward is a fight.

tertiary_outcast.name: Lesser beasts
tertiary_outcast.worldview: They live where the water has gone wrong and answer to no one.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: They are numerous, fill gaps in the corridors, and cannot easily be bargained with.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: They have no plan and break when their demon masters fall.

output_dial.level_1: A quiet crawl through the rock corridors, with a few lesser beasts and a foul smell from the water.
output_dial.level_2: Fallen ones ambush the arrival point, and Goat Demons hold the corridors between the party and the spring.
output_dial.level_3: The infestation is thick in every corridor, the water is dangerously tainted, and retreat to the crack is contested.
output_dial.level_4: The cavern is a demon stronghold: the spring is poisoned beyond cleansing, the way back is cut off, and the party is trapped in the dark.

threat_clocks.name: The taint spreads
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party lingers, fights loudly, or lets demons fall into the water.

yields_resource: The party gains a cleared dark passage, whatever lore or loot the marked entrance hid, and the chance to end the spring's fouling.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: A crack in a wall of the second depth, framed with ornaments normally kept for important tomes, leads to caverns where a spring has been fouled by demons. Fallen ones wait at the arrival point. The route is a few rock corridors of Goat Demons and lesser beasts, so it is a compact set piece.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place it as a side branch off a dungeon level, found by a party that investigates odd wall decoration. It consumes a light source and an appetite for lore. It feeds any plot about tainted water, demon spread, or hidden passages. Arrival goes well when the party scouts the entrance and meets the fallen ones prepared. It goes badly when they walk in blind, are ambushed, and are caught between the beasts and the poisoned water.

title: The Fouled Spring Beneath the Dungeon
summary: Behind a crack in the wall, a set-piece cavern holds Goat Demons and lesser beasts that foul the town's water. Clearing them cleanses the spring, and Pepin rewards the hero with the Ring of Truth.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-shot cavern clearing. The party finds a hidden crack in a dungeon wall, fights the demons and beasts in the caverns beyond, and when the last falls the fouled water runs clear and a grateful healer gives a reward.
premise: A town that needs clean water + monsters poisoning the source below = a hero must clear the caverns to restore it.

sensory.physical_environment: Set-piece caverns beyond a crack labeled 'To A Dark Passage'. A fouled waterway runs through them.
sensory.behaviors: The party kills Goat Demons and lesser beasts through the whole level. When the last monster falls, a trumpet of triumph sounds in the distance.
sensory.relationships: The healer Pepin depends on the hero to restore the town's water, and rewards success.
sensory.attitudes: Relief and triumph at the end, after grim, dirty fighting in the dark.
sensory.values: Public good, the cleansing of what has been defiled, and gratitude for the deed.

establishment.name: Pepin
establishment.worldview: A healer who knows the town's sickness has a source and trusts the hero to remove it.
establishment.leverage: The Ring of Truth, as a reward, and his standing among the townsfolk.
establishment.flaw: He can only wait for others to act.

main_opponent.name: The Goat Demons
main_opponent.worldview: Brutes that hold the caverns as their own.
main_opponent.leverage: Strength in the dark, and their hold over the water source.
main_opponent.flaw: They are territorial and fixed to the caverns, with no strategy beyond defense.

thematic_shadow.name: The lesser beasts of the caverns
thematic_shadow.worldview: Creatures that feed on the corruption seeping through the water.
thematic_shadow.leverage: Numbers and surprise in tight passages.
thematic_shadow.flaw: They are driven by instinct and scatter when their leaders fall.

tertiary_outcast.name: A townsperson who drinks the water regardless
tertiary_outcast.worldview: There is no other well, so the risk must be accepted.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: Their illness is a visible warning of the cost of delay.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: They cannot act, only suffer.

output_dial.level_1: The party finds the crack, clears the caverns without much trouble, and the water runs clear.
output_dial.level_2: The Goat Demons and beasts put up a hard fight through the whole level, and the party emerges victorious.
output_dial.level_3: The caverns are a long gauntlet and the party is worn down, with the poisoned town waiting for relief.
output_dial.level_4: The party is lost in the dark passages, the spring stays fouled, and the town's sickness spreads.

threat_clocks.name: The Town Sickens
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party delays the clearing and the poisoned water continues to flow.

yields_resource: A cleansed water supply and the Ring of Truth from Pepin.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: A set-piece cavern lies behind a crack in the wall. The party kills Goat Demons and lesser beasts. When the last monster falls, a trumpet of triumph sounds and the fouled waterway clears to blue before their eyes. Pepin then gives the Ring of Truth.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place it just below an early dungeon level, reached through a hidden or marked crack. It consumes the party's strength and supplies, and feeds the town's wellbeing and a valuable reward. It goes well when the clearing feels like a real purge, with the water change as a visible payoff. It goes badly if the party skips the crack or leaves monsters alive, since the victory only comes when the last one falls.

title: Potions of Healing and Mana
summary: Nearly every restorative in Tristram comes from the Healer or the Witch. Using them well is an economic puzzle of gold, pack space and what kind of fighter you are.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a shopping scene in a besieged town. Two merchants sell restoratives, the party's purse and carrying room are limited, and each character must decide which mix of healing and mana to carry before descending.
premise: A fighter who wants a single flawless cure + a purse that cannot afford it = a hard choice between convenience and a smarter, cheaper mix of potions.

sensory.physical_environment: Crowded shelves and bottles at the Healer's and the Witch's stalls in Tristram, with a few stray potions in the dungeon below.
sensory.behaviors: Adventurers haggle, weigh their purses, count the free slots in their packs and stock different mixes of potions to suit their class.
sensory.relationships: Pepin the Healer and Adria the Witch are the two suppliers a character depends on, and each class leans on one of them more heavily.
sensory.attitudes: Prudent shoppers see the single all-in-one potion as flashy and wasteful, and a cross-section of cheaper potions as the wiser purchase.
sensory.values: Thrift, preparedness and fitting your supplies to your own nature.

establishment.name: Pepin the Healer
establishment.worldview: Restoring the wounded is honest, steady work that keeps the town alive.
establishment.leverage: He is the main source of healing potions.
establishment.flaw: He can only sell what adventurers can pay for.

main_opponent.name: Adria the Witch
main_opponent.worldview: Mana is the real currency of power, and she sells it on her own terms.
main_opponent.leverage: She controls the supply of mana potions that casters rely on.
main_opponent.flaw: Her customers can swap in cheaper mixes or healing magic instead.

thematic_shadow.name: The spendthrift fighter
thematic_shadow.worldview: One perfect potion beats any fiddly arrangement.
thematic_shadow.leverage: Convenience and a fully restored character in a single swallow.
thematic_shadow.flaw: The costly potion is, by the guide's own verdict, a bad investment.

tertiary_outcast.name: The rogue who hedges
tertiary_outcast.worldview: Health and mana are balanced, and equipment may change at any time, so no stock is ever final.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: A flexible kit that suits whatever turns up in the dungeon.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: A mixed kit is never ideal for any single situation.

output_dial.level_1: The party restocks without trouble, buying a sensible mix that fits each character.
output_dial.level_2: Purses run thin and packs fill up, so characters must pick which potions to leave behind.
output_dial.level_3: A character who overspent on the costly all-in-one potion runs out of one resource mid-fight and cannot afford a replacement.
output_dial.level_4: The party is deep in the dungeon with wasted gold and mismatched potions, and no way to recover one meter when it matters most.

threat_clocks.name: Purse runs dry
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party buys the expensive all-in-one potion or a poorly matched mix instead of a cheaper tailored one.

yields_resource: A well-matched kit of restoratives that covers both health and mana at lower cost, plus the know-how to rebuild it as equipment changes.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: Apart from a few quest-specific elixirs, nearly all potions come from the Healer and the Witch. The challenge is economic: what the purse can afford, how much the pack can hold, and what the character's class actually needs. The all-in-one potion is the tidiest answer, but the guide calls it a bad investment and advises mixing a full potion of one kind with a partial one of the other.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place this in Tristram as a downtime or resupply scene before a descent, ideally in the mid-to-late game when purses are fuller. It consumes the party's gold and carrying space, and it feeds every dangerous encounter that follows. An arrival goes well when characters plan around their own class and keep a varied kit; it goes badly when they chase the single flashy purchase and are caught short.
