title: Procedural Dungeons and Fixed Geography
summary: The dungeons and caves generate randomly while Tristram's geography remains constant.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a base-and-descent scenario. Fix Tristram as a map the party can trust, generate each underground level fresh as they enter it, and let them use the direct avenues back to the town whenever they need to recover.
premise: Delvers who want a reliable plan + an underworld that never repeats itself = they must rely on one constant place and their own judgement below.

sensory.physical_environment: Dungeons and caves beneath the earth that generate randomly, set against a town whose geography remains constant.
sensory.behaviors: Delvers push downward without a fail-safe guide, then use direct avenues even from deep underground back to Tristram.
sensory.relationships: The town is the fixed point to which every random descent is tied.
sensory.attitudes: No one claims a single best route, and no guide offers fail-safe solutions.
sensory.values: Judgement over formula, with a dependable home to return to.

establishment.name: Tristram
establishment.worldview: A fixed home gives meaning to every uncertain journey out of it.
establishment.leverage: Its constant geography and the direct avenues leading back to it.
establishment.flaw: It cannot predict or control what the dungeons below will become.

main_opponent.name: The Randomized Depths
main_opponent.worldview: No path is repeated, so no path can be relied on.
main_opponent.leverage: Layouts that change and thereby defeat any memorized solution.
main_opponent.flaw: They are bounded by the fixed ground above and by the routes that lead back to it.

thematic_shadow.name: The Route-Planner (a delver who seeks the single best way)
thematic_shadow.worldview: With enough study, a perfect route through the game must exist.
thematic_shadow.leverage: Experience and confidence that make familiar stretches efficient.
thematic_shadow.flaw: The randomness defeats the idea that any one best route exists.

tertiary_outcast.name: The Stranded Delver (a hero lost far underground)
tertiary_outcast.worldview: Home is far away, and the way back may not be obvious.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: First-hand knowledge of how deep the dungeon goes and what it costs.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: Overlooking the direct avenues that lead back to Tristram.

output_dial.level_1: The party moves easily between the constant town and a fresh level, and treats the random layout as a pleasant puzzle.
output_dial.level_2: Unfamiliar passages slow the party, and they lean on the town as a reliable place to regroup and resupply.
output_dial.level_3: The party is deep, the layout is unfamiliar and prior notes are useless, so they must find a direct avenue back before their resources fail.
output_dial.level_4: The party is lost in a level that matches nothing they know, cut off from supplies and uncertain how to reach the way home.

threat_clocks.name: Lost Below
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party presses deeper without noting the direct avenues back to Tristram, or relies on a guide's route that no longer holds.

threat_clocks.name: False Certainty
threat_clocks.advances_when: A player insists a fail-safe solution exists and acts on it despite the layout having changed.

yields_resource: A dependable anchor in Tristram, knowledge of the direct avenues home, and the party's growing skill at reading unfamiliar ground.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: The dungeons and caves beneath the earth generate randomly, yet Tristram's geography remains constant. Because of the randomness, no guide can offer fail-safe solutions and no single best route through the game exists. Direct avenues exist even from deep underground back to Tristram. Use this pairing of fixed surface and shifting depths to give the party both uncertainty and a way home.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place this as the structural backbone of a campaign: Tristram is the stable hub, and every descent branches from it. It consumes the party's wish for certainty and feeds modules about the dungeon, the heroes and the reshuffling world, since all of them benefit from a fixed point of return. An arrival goes well when the party respects the constant town and uses the direct avenues to recover. It goes badly when they trust an old route, or forget that a way back exists, and spend their strength wandering.

title: Randomly Generated Dungeon World
summary: The game's world is generated randomly: levels, weapons, monsters and the cast of characters change each time the game is started, so the same play-through is never repeated.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-shot descent. Before play, shuffle the layout, the foes and the loot with random tables, and let the party learn each new level only by entering it. Nothing is carried over from a previous run, and no map is trusted.
premise: Adventurers who rely on known routes and familiar foes + a world that reshuffles itself every time = they must win, buy or barter new means and learn each threat anew.

sensory.physical_environment: Labyrinthine levels and cavernous grottos whose layout is different each time the game starts.
sensory.behaviors: Delvers win, buy or barter armaments and magic spells, then learn to use them against a long list of foes.
sensory.relationships: The cast of characters shuffles, so allies and enemies shift between runs. Friends or enemies can also join over the Net.
sensory.attitudes: No play-through repeats, so confidence in past experience is misplaced. Every descent is treated as a first one.
sensory.values: Adaptability, resourcefulness and skill matter more than memorized solutions.

establishment.name: The Dungeon Itself (as the generating order)
establishment.worldview: The depths remake themselves so that no one can master them once and for all.
establishment.leverage: Control over what is found, who is met and where the passages lead.
establishment.flaw: It offers no stable ground, so even its own agents cannot predict its next shape.

main_opponent.name: The Long List of Foes
main_opponent.worldview: Every delver is prey, and the roster of monsters shifts to keep them off balance.
main_opponent.leverage: Variety and surprise: the party never knows exactly what waits below.
main_opponent.flaw: They are only as dangerous as the party's lack of preparation and adaptability.

thematic_shadow.name: The Guide-Seeker (a delver who wants a fail-safe route)
thematic_shadow.worldview: A single best solution must exist if only someone writes it down.
thematic_shadow.leverage: Shared notes, habit and confidence that save effort on familiar ground.
thematic_shadow.flaw: Their certainty fails the moment the world reshuffles.

tertiary_outcast.name: The Barterer (a merchant of arms and spells)
tertiary_outcast.worldview: Everything is a trade, and what a delver lacks can be bought if the price is met.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: Access to the armaments and magic spells that delvers need.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: Their stock is only as good as the party's coin and their willingness to deal.

output_dial.level_1: The shuffle is a curiosity: new rooms, a few unfamiliar foes and some odd finds keep the party alert but comfortable.
output_dial.level_2: The reshuffle bites: the party's chosen weapons and spells do not suit the foes that appear, and they must trade or improvise to keep going.
output_dial.level_3: The world turns hostile to habit: plans fail repeatedly, supplies run thin and the party is forced to relearn how to fight as the cast around them changes.
output_dial.level_4: Nothing known survives: the party enters a level wholly unlike any expectation, unprepared and underequipped, and the descent threatens to end them.

threat_clocks.name: Preparation Eroded
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party relies on past knowledge, a stale map or a familiar tactic that the reshuffled world no longer honors.

threat_clocks.name: Arsenal Mismatch
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party meets foes their current arms and spells cannot answer, and has no chance to win, buy or barter replacements.

yields_resource: Fresh armaments and magic spells won, bought or bartered along the way, plus hard-won knowledge of a threat the party has now learned to counter.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: The dungeon world is built fresh each time the game starts. Levels, weapons, monsters and nearly everything else are generated randomly, the cast shuffles and the possibilities shift. Whether the party plays as Rogue, Warrior or Sorcerer, each run is its own story. At the table, treat the shuffle as the point: the party must win, buy or barter for what they need and learn each foe as it comes, and the difficulty can be raised to suit their skill.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place this as the framing condition of a whole descent rather than a single location. It consumes the party's assumptions and rewards improvisation, and it feeds any module that supplies foes, trade or loot, since all of those can be rolled fresh. It pairs naturally with the fixed-geography concept so that Tristram stays a stable anchor above the churn. An arrival goes well when the party treats each level as new, trades smartly and adapts. It goes badly when they cling to a plan from a past descent and discover it no longer applies.

title: Rising Sun Inn and Tavern
summary: Ogden's inn and tavern, whose hanging sign was stolen by demons.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-scene hook. The party arrives at a tavern whose owner is upset that demons stole his hanging sign, and they may be hired to recover it.
premise: A tavern keeper who wants his town's ordinary life back + demons who steal even his sign = a small, personal quest that shows the larger evil.

sensory.physical_environment: An inn and tavern with an empty spot where its hanging sign should be.
sensory.behaviors: Ogden runs the house and talks about the sign that demons took.
sensory.relationships: Ogden owns the establishment. The demons are the cause of its loss.
sensory.attitudes: The theft is a petty, mocking insult to a place of ordinary comfort.
sensory.values: Hospitality, normal life, and the dignity of a local landmark.

establishment.name: Ogden the Tavern Owner
establishment.worldview: The inn is the heart of the town and its name should hang over the door.
establishment.leverage: He owns the inn, gives lodging and hears the town's talk.
establishment.flaw: He is not a fighter and depends on outsiders to recover what was taken.

main_opponent.name: The demons who stole the sign
main_opponent.worldview: Taking even small things shows the town that nothing is safe.
main_opponent.leverage: They have already taken the sign, and nobody in town has been able to get it back.
main_opponent.flaw: Their petty theft leaves a trail that can be followed.

thematic_shadow.name: The anxious townsfolk
thematic_shadow.worldview: Keep your head down and hope the evil passes.
thematic_shadow.leverage: They bring rumor and gossip to the inn.
thematic_shadow.flaw: Fear makes them unwilling to help.

tertiary_outcast.name: A wandering patron
tertiary_outcast.worldview: A tavern is a place to hear a story and move on.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: They carry news from elsewhere and owe the place no loyalty.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: They will not stay to see the problem solved.

output_dial.level_1: Ogden grumbles about his missing sign, and the inn is otherwise open and warm.
output_dial.level_2: The loss of the sign sours the mood, regulars drift away, and Ogden asks the party to find it.
output_dial.level_3: The demons return to take more from the inn, and the town begins to see the theft as a sign of worse to come.
output_dial.level_4: The inn is abandoned or overrun, and its fall marks the end of safe, ordinary life in town.

threat_clocks.name: The Town Loses Heart
threat_clocks.advances_when: The sign stays missing and the demons act again unchallenged.

yields_resource: Recovering the sign earns Ogden's gratitude, a safe place to rest, and the goodwill and rumors of the town.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: Ogden's Rising Sun Inn and Tavern lost its hanging sign to demons. Little else is established, so the small theft carries the story: the evil reaches even the humble things in town.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Use it as the town's social hub and early quest-giver, near the start of play. It consumes the party's attention and feeds them rumors, lodging and a modest quest. The card names no further links, so any connection to other places is the GM's choice. An arrival goes well when the party treats the sign as worth recovering and so earns Ogden's trust. It goes badly if the party dismisses the theft and the town's morale keeps sinking.

title: Ruined Cathedral at the Edge of the Village
summary: A ruined cathedral at the edge of a somber, twilit village, where the townsfolk say strange rituals are performed. Dim light seeps from its church doorway, and inside a stone stairway plunges into darkness toward a dungeon.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-shot threshold scene. The party arrives at a twilit village, hears of rituals in the ruined cathedral, meets a dying man at the church door, and must decide whether to take the stairway down.
premise: A hero who answers a frightened village's plea + a cathedral where evil rituals lead down into death = a descent no one can walk back from unchanged.

sensory.physical_environment: A somber, twilit village. Dim light seeps from the church doorway, and a stone stairway plunges into darkness toward a dungeon where the scent of death surrounds the hero.
sensory.behaviors: A dying man writhes in agony at the church entrance. The townsfolk speak of invasion by dark riders and of strange rituals performed in the ruin.
sensory.relationships: The cathedral stands at the village edge and connects to the dungeon beneath it. The dwindling villagers fear it and cannot stop what happens there.
sensory.attitudes: Somber, evil and anxious.
sensory.values: Survival and warning over bravery. The village wants someone else to face the evil.

establishment.name: The anxious and dwindling populace
establishment.worldview: The evil is real and the village cannot fight it.
establishment.leverage: They know the rumors of dark riders and strange rituals, and they have been watching the cathedral.
establishment.flaw: They are frightened and shrinking, and cannot act on what they know.

main_opponent.name: The dark riders and ritual performers
main_opponent.worldview: The village and its people are there to be invaded and consumed.
main_opponent.leverage: They have invaded the area and use the ruin for strange rituals.
main_opponent.flaw: Their nature is not immediately clear, which leaves room for the party to learn what they are before they strike.

thematic_shadow.name: The dying man at the entrance
thematic_shadow.worldview: He is a warning of what the cathedral does to those who go in.
thematic_shadow.leverage: His suffering shows the stakes without a word of explanation.
thematic_shadow.flaw: He is dying and can give only fragments.

tertiary_outcast.name: Whatever haunts the dungeon below
tertiary_outcast.worldview: Death is the only welcome the descent offers.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: The scent of death surrounds all who go down the stairway.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: It is far below, so the party meets it only if it chooses to descend.

output_dial.level_1: The village is gloomy and rumor-ridden, the doorway glows dimly, and the party can study the ruin from outside.
output_dial.level_2: The dying man and the villagers' warnings press the party toward the cathedral, and the stairway beckons.
output_dial.level_3: The rituals and the dark riders make the village's decline plain, and the party must act or watch it empty.
output_dial.level_4: The village is lost or the party is trapped on the stairway, with the scent of death leaving no doubt about what lies below.

threat_clocks.name: The Village Empties
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party delays, and the dark riders and rituals continue unopposed.

threat_clocks.name: The Rituals Complete
threat_clocks.advances_when: The ruin's strange rituals proceed without interruption.

yields_resource: Dealing with the cathedral gives the party the villagers' trust and information, and access to the stairway down into the dungeon.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: The ruined cathedral at the village edge is where the evil is first felt. The villagers speak of dark riders and strange rituals, a dying man writhes at the entrance, dim light seeps from the doorway, and a stone stairway plunges into darkness toward a dungeon that smells of death.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place it at the start of the adventure as the threshold between the village and the dungeon beneath the cathedral. It consumes the party's first impressions and nerve, and it feeds them the rumors, the warning of the dying man and the way down. An arrival goes well when the party gathers what the villagers know and takes the stairway prepared. It goes badly when they ignore the warnings and descend unready, or treat the dying man as scenery.

title: Save Before Accessing a Shrine
summary: A shrine in the dungeon offers an unknown boon or burden, and the wise delegate pauses to weigh it before committing.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-shot: the party finds a lone shrine in a dark chamber. Before anyone touches it, let them take a moment to consider, scout, and debate. Then reveal its effect and let them live with the consequences.
premise: Cautious adventurers + a shrine whose effects are binding once touched = a tense decision made with incomplete knowledge.

sensory.physical_environment: A shrine set within the dungeon, quiet and waiting.
sensory.behaviors: Adventurers hesitate, weigh the choice, and prepare before they commit.
sensory.relationships: The guide's advice passes from experience to newcomer; the shrine is a silent counterpart.
sensory.attitudes: Prudence and wariness toward effects that cannot be undone.
sensory.values: Consider effects before committing to them.

establishment.name: The guide
establishment.worldview: Preparation and foresight keep adventurers alive.
establishment.leverage: Accumulated experience and advice.
establishment.flaw: Its counsel cannot remove the risk itself.

main_opponent.name: The shrine
main_opponent.worldview: Its effects take hold once accessed, for good or ill.
main_opponent.leverage: Uncertainty and the lure of power.
main_opponent.flaw: It is passive and only acts when touched.

thematic_shadow.name: The reckless delver
thematic_shadow.worldview: Fortune favors those who grab it at once.
thematic_shadow.leverage: Speed and boldness.
thematic_shadow.flaw: Bears the full cost of any bad outcome.

tertiary_outcast.name: A party member who refuses to touch any shrine
tertiary_outcast.worldview: Unknown power is never worth the price.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: Can veto or delay the group.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: Forfeits benefits the others might gain.

output_dial.level_1: The shrine's effect is mild or helpful and the party chooses calmly after discussion.
output_dial.level_2: The effect is a real trade-off and the party argues over whether to accept it.
output_dial.level_3: The effect is harmful or hampers the party, and they must press on with a lasting cost.
output_dial.level_4: A rash choice binds the party to a ruinous effect with no way to reverse it, shaping the rest of the descent.

threat_clocks.name: Commitment to the Unknown
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party rushes, ignores precautions, or touches the shrine without weighing its possible effects.

yields_resource: Foreknowledge and a deliberate choice: the party gains the shrine's effect on terms they chose with open eyes.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: The guide advises doing one thing before accessing a shrine in the dungeon: prepare so the effects can be considered before committing. The situation dramatizes that pause and what follows from it.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place it as a quiet chamber partway through a dungeon, ideally after a fight so the party feels vulnerable and tempted. It consumes the party's caution and feeds whatever the shrine grants or costs. It goes well when the party scouts, discusses, and chooses together; it goes badly when impatience commits them to an effect they did not weigh. Specific shrine effects are the GM's invention, as the card names none.

title: Servants of Darkness
summary: The vast host of dungeon monsters, unique horrors with a single purpose, which is to kill. They fall into Undead, Animal-based monsters and Demons, and are served up by category and template.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a single encounter table. Pick one of three families (Undead, Animal-based, Demon), build a monster from a template in that family, and place it where the party must pass.
premise: Monsters bred for nothing but killing + heroes who must cross their territory = every room is a test of the party's endurance.

sensory.physical_environment: The subterranean lands of Tristram, filled with flesh-eating demons, rotting corpses and winged beasties.
sensory.behaviors: They lurch, swarm and flutter through the dungeon, and kill is their one aim.
sensory.relationships: They serve Diablo, who commands them, and they inhabit the dungeon. Undead, Animal-based monsters and Demons are their three families.
sensory.attitudes: Relentless, mindless hostility.
sensory.values: Killing is the only purpose, and nothing else counts.

establishment.name: Diablo
establishment.worldview: The monsters are his army, existing to kill on his behalf.
establishment.leverage: He commands them and they serve him.
establishment.flaw: His power rests on servants who have no loyalty beyond killing.

main_opponent.name: The delving heroes
main_opponent.worldview: The host must be fought through to restore the world above.
main_opponent.leverage: Skill, preparation and the chance to pick their battles.
main_opponent.flaw: They are outnumbered by a host built to kill.

thematic_shadow.name: The Demons
thematic_shadow.worldview: They are the purest form of the dungeon's malice.
thematic_shadow.leverage: Raw menace and a place of command within the host.
thematic_shadow.flaw: They are bound to a master and a single purpose.

tertiary_outcast.name: The Animal-based monsters
tertiary_outcast.worldview: They are beasts twisted into killers and sit apart from the Undead and Demons.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: They are the host's most natural fauna.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: They are the least bound by any higher purpose, so they are the easiest to read.

output_dial.level_1: A few scattered servants turn up as routine hazards of the descent.
output_dial.level_2: Groups of one family, such as Undead, Animal-based or Demon, contest the party's route and demand tactics.
output_dial.level_3: Mixed families swarm the party, and the dungeon feels like one hostile organism.
output_dial.level_4: The full host converges and the party faces an unbroken tide with no safe ground.

threat_clocks.name: The Host Gathers
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party makes noise, lingers in one place, or leaves earlier encounters unresolved.

yields_resource: Knowledge of each monster family's habits, and safer passage through the dungeon once a family's pattern is understood.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: The Servants of Darkness are a very large host of unique horrors with one purpose, which is to kill. They are grouped into Undead, Animal-based monsters and Demons, and refined into templates. Which monster appears is chosen randomly or by the depth of the level, so treat the host as a generator rather than a fixed cast.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Use it as the standing background for any dungeon. It consumes Diablo's command and a habitat, and it feeds encounters, garrisons and lore about the dungeon. Link it to the dungeon module. It goes well when each family has a recognizable feel and the party can learn to read it. It goes badly when every fight is the same swarm and the variety of templates is lost.

title: Shrine Inscriptions
summary: Every shrine speaks a riddling message that hints at what it will do, and the table supplies the translation. Some messages split between 'You' and 'Others', showing who the shrine's effect lands on.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-shot puzzle at a single shrine. The GM reads the inscription aloud, the players argue over what it means and who it affects, and then someone commits to touching it. The GM reveals the true effect, with a boon and a cost that match the riddle.
premise: Characters who gamble on cryptic promises + a shrine that tells the truth only in riddles = power won or lost by how well the table reads it

sensory.physical_environment: A lone shrine in a dim, hostile place, its message spoken or etched where adventurers cannot miss it.
sensory.behaviors: Travelers stop, repeat the line aloud, argue over its meaning, and hesitate before touching the shrine.
sensory.relationships: Some messages address 'You' and 'Others' separately, so a shrine can favor the one who touches it or the companions beside them.
sensory.attitudes: Suspicion and temptation. Every line sounds like wisdom and also like a trap.
sensory.values: Strength forged through destruction, wisdom traded for power, and the idea that nothing is gained without a price.

establishment.name: The shrine's voice
establishment.worldview: Truth is offered freely, but only to those who can read it.
establishment.leverage: It always tells the truth in some form, so careful readers can profit.
establishment.flaw: Its riddles are ambiguous, and the same words can support opposite readings.

main_opponent.name: The reckless toucher
main_opponent.worldview: Power is for whoever grabs it first.
main_opponent.leverage: Speed and nerve; they act while others are still debating.
main_opponent.flaw: They ignore the warning in the words and pay for it.

thematic_shadow.name: The over-reader
thematic_shadow.worldview: Every phrase hides a precise instruction, and a clever enough mind can decode it.
thematic_shadow.leverage: Patient analysis can spot real tradeoffs.
thematic_shadow.flaw: They invent meaning and miss the plain one, such as 'Wherever you go, there you are'.

tertiary_outcast.name: The companion left out
tertiary_outcast.worldview: Boons meant for 'Others' should not depend on a leader's gamble.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: They can refuse to follow, or demand a say before anyone touches the shrine.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: They have no way to check a riddle, so they rely on trust.

output_dial.level_1: The shrine's message is a mild curiosity, and the effect is a small, welcome boon that matches a plain reading.
output_dial.level_2: The message hints at a real tradeoff, and the effect gives something useful while taking something in return.
output_dial.level_3: The message hides a harsh bargain, and a misreading leaves the party weakened at a bad moment.
output_dial.level_4: A mistaken reading ruins a character or splits the party, and the shrine's cost cannot be undone.

threat_clocks.name: The Gamble Closes In
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party debates in the open while threats gather, a shrine is touched without discussion, or a riddle is misread.

yields_resource: A boon of strength, insight or fortune, and a clearer grasp of how the world's shrines trade power for cost.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: Each shrine speaks a riddle that hints at its effect, and the table provides the translation. Lines like 'New strength is forged through destruction', 'Those who defend seldom attack' and 'Some are weakened as one grows strong' point to a tradeoff. Messages that split between 'You' and 'Others' show who the effect targets. Players decide how much to trust the hint before they commit.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place a shrine in a quiet pause between fights, or at a decision point where a party under pressure might gamble. It feeds on any location that can host a shrine and gives back a boon or a cost for the next scene. An arrival goes well when the GM keeps the riddle clear enough to read, the cost matches the wording, and the party's discussion matters. It goes badly if the riddle is arbitrary, the effect contradicts the words, or one player decides for everyone.

title: Snotspill's Set Piece
summary: A small set-piece area on Dungeon Level 4, between the player and the staircase down to Level 5. Snotspill waits here, and the large chest holding the tavern sign is here, guarded by several massive monsters.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-shot boss room. The party must clear a small chamber held by Snotspill, his friends and several massive monsters to open the large chest and reach the stair down.
premise: Heroes who need the way down + a chokepoint held by Snotspill and massive guardians = a fight that must be won to reach the chest and the stair

sensory.physical_environment: A small set-piece area on the way to the staircase down, with a large chest at its centre.
sensory.behaviors: Snotspill waits here with his friends. Several massive monsters stand guard over the chest.
sensory.relationships: Snotspill leads his friends and the massive guardians. The chest is tied to the tavern sign quest.
sensory.attitudes: They are waiting, so the party is expected, and the place is defended.
sensory.values: The chest is worth defending and the stair is the prize. Nothing passes without a fight.

establishment.name: Snotspill and his friends
establishment.worldview: This small area is theirs, and anyone heading for the stair has to deal with them.
establishment.leverage: They wait ready on ground they chose, between the party and the way down.
establishment.flaw: They are tied to the spot and are cornered by a party that forces the fight.

main_opponent.name: The massive monsters
main_opponent.worldview: They exist to guard the large chest and kill what approaches it.
main_opponent.leverage: Their size and number make the room dangerous to rush.
main_opponent.flaw: They guard a fixed point, so they can be drawn off or fought one at a time.

thematic_shadow.name: The tavern sign chest
thematic_shadow.worldview: What is lost can be recovered, but only at a cost.
thematic_shadow.leverage: The contents tie a quest to the room, so the party has to take it.
thematic_shadow.flaw: It is bait, and the party is tempted to push on past what it can handle.

tertiary_outcast.name: The descending adventurer
tertiary_outcast.worldview: They only want the staircase down and have no stake in the chest.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: They can skip the sign and press on to the stair.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: They cannot reach the stair without clearing the room first.

output_dial.level_1: Snotspill and his friends are quickly beaten and the guards are thin, leaving the chest easy to open.
output_dial.level_2: Snotspill and the massive monsters hold the area, and the party fights to open the chest and reach the stair.
output_dial.level_3: The massive monsters swarm the room, Snotspill's friends flank the party, and the chest and stair are both out of reach.
output_dial.level_4: The party is overwhelmed in the small chamber with no retreat, and the chest and stair stay out of reach.

threat_clocks.name: The guards close in
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party fights in the open or fails to split Snotspill's friends from the massive monsters.

yields_resource: The party gains the large chest with the tavern sign, and passage to the staircase down.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: A small set-piece area sits between the party and the staircase down. Snotspill waits here with his friends, and the large chest holding the tavern sign is guarded by several massive monsters. The area must be cleared to reach the stair.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place it as the last obstacle before descending. It consumes the party's strength and the quest hook for the tavern sign, and it feeds the sign quest and the next descent. Arrival goes well when the party scouts, separates Snotspill from the guards, and claims the chest. It goes badly when they rush in, the massive monsters pin them, and the stair stays out of reach.

title: Sorcery and Magic in Diablo
summary: Magic is framed as the defining power of the Diablo experience, whether wielded by a Sorcerer or granted by shrines. Sorcerers rely on magic and Mana most, and their spell levels and Mana economy scale faster than those of Warriors or Rogues, who find scrolls and books mostly useless and are better off selling them.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a magical-power scene: one caster shows how awesome magic can be through spells or a shrine's boon. Non-casters realize scrolls and books are only trade goods for them.
premise: A caster who lives by Mana + a world where magic is both awesome and double-edged = they must manage a growing power that others cannot share.

sensory.physical_environment: The tremendous power of magic, brought to bear by a mighty Sorcerer or bestowed at one of the many shrines.
sensory.behaviors: Sorcerers pour spells and Mana into the fight while Warriors and Rogues set aside scrolls and books to sell.
sensory.relationships: Casters and non-casters stand apart, since a Sorcerer's spell levels and Mana economy grow at a much greater rate than those of the others.
sensory.attitudes: Awe at magic that is often awesome, edged with the suspicion of smoke and mirrors.
sensory.values: Understanding and proper use of the game's magical components is essential.

establishment.name: The Sorcerer
establishment.worldview: Magic is the meat and potatoes of the experience.
establishment.leverage: Spell levels, Mana economy and damage that scale faster than other classes.
establishment.flaw: Depends on Mana and on understanding the magical components well.

main_opponent.name: Those who face a caster's magic
main_opponent.worldview: Sorcery is the great threat that overshadows mundane arms.
main_opponent.leverage: They can exploit a caster's Mana limits.
main_opponent.flaw: They lack comparable scaling.

thematic_shadow.name: The shrines
thematic_shadow.worldview: Magic can be bestowed without study.
thematic_shadow.leverage: They grant power to any who approach.
thematic_shadow.flaw: Their boons arrive unasked and may come as smoke and mirrors.

tertiary_outcast.name: Warriors and Rogues
tertiary_outcast.worldview: Scrolls and books are mostly useless and best sold.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: They convert unused magic into coin.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: They are locked out of the greatest power the world offers.

output_dial.level_1: A caster uses a few spells or a shrine's boon to ease a routine challenge.
output_dial.level_2: Magic visibly turns the tide as a Sorcerer's growing spell levels outpace the other classes.
output_dial.level_3: Mana runs low or a shrine's effect proves treacherous, leaving the party reliant on a caster who is nearly spent.
output_dial.level_4: Unchecked magic or a failed spell becomes the crisis itself, and the power the party relied on turns against them.

threat_clocks.name: Mana Runs Dry
threat_clocks.advances_when: The caster spends Mana without rest or restoration, or the party leans on magic for every problem.

yields_resource: Understanding of the magical components and awesome magical power, plus coin from scrolls and books the non-casters sell.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: Magic is one of the most significant aspects of the experience: its power is tremendous, wielded by a mighty Sorcerer or bestowed at shrines, and the proper understanding of its components is essential. A Sorcerer's spell levels, with the resulting Mana economy and damage, grow much faster than those of Warriors or Rogues, who find scrolls and books mostly useless.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Use this as the framing for any magic-heavy scene or as a late-delve showcase of power. It consumes Mana and spellcasting knowledge and feeds item-property and loot hooks. An arrival goes well when the Sorcerer shines and others profit by selling unused scrolls. It goes badly when the party depends on spent Mana or cannot use the magic they find.

title: The Three Heroes
summary: Players guide one of three distinct characters through the dungeons beneath Tristram.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a character-choice opening. Offer the table three distinct delver archetypes (the Rogue, the Warrior and the Sorcerer), let each player claim one, and send them into a single labyrinthine descent where their differences shape every problem.
premise: A delver who must commit to one of three distinct paths + a labyrinth that treats each path differently = a choice that shapes the whole descent.

sensory.physical_environment: Labyrinthine dungeons and cavernous grottos carved deep in the earth near Tristram.
sensory.behaviors: The player guides one chosen character downward, and a Sorcerer is advised to check the Witch's supply before other purchases.
sensory.relationships: Each hero is distinct, and the Sorcerer in particular depends on the Witch's stock to prepare.
sensory.attitudes: Choosing a hero is a commitment that sets how the descent will feel.
sensory.values: Preparation suited to one's chosen role, and trust in a specialist supplier.

establishment.name: Tristram
establishment.worldview: The town above is the stable base from which delvers set out and to which they should be able to return.
establishment.leverage: Supplies, shelter and the Witch's stock that the Sorcerer relies on.
establishment.flaw: It can only support delvers, not descend and fight for them.

main_opponent.name: The Dungeons Beneath Tristram
main_opponent.worldview: The labyrinth tests each hero differently and gives no quarter to any role.
main_opponent.leverage: Winding passages and grottos that punish unsuited preparation.
main_opponent.flaw: It cannot stop a hero whose role is well matched to the challenge.

thematic_shadow.name: The Rival Hero (another archetype in the same descent)
thematic_shadow.worldview: My chosen path is the right one, and the others are lesser versions of it.
thematic_shadow.leverage: A distinct set of strengths that complements or competes with the party.
thematic_shadow.flaw: A single archetype alone cannot answer every problem the depths present.

tertiary_outcast.name: The Witch
tertiary_outcast.worldview: Magic must be stocked before it is needed, and a Sorcerer who forgets will pay for it.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: Control over the supply that a Sorcerer must check first.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: Her usefulness is narrow, since non-casters need little from her.

output_dial.level_1: The chosen hero fits the early dungeon well, and the player enjoys the sense of a role well played.
output_dial.level_2: The hero's limits start to show: some obstacles favor the Rogue, the Warrior or the Sorcerer, and the player must lean on strengths and cover weaknesses.
output_dial.level_3: The hero is poorly matched to the depths ahead, supplies are mis-prioritized and the player feels the cost of a hasty choice.
output_dial.level_4: The chosen path collapses: the Sorcerer is caught without the Witch's stock, or a hero faces a threat that their role simply cannot answer, and the expedition faces ruin.

threat_clocks.name: Unsuited Preparation
threat_clocks.advances_when: A hero descends without purchases fitting their role, such as a Sorcerer who skips the Witch's supply.

threat_clocks.name: Role Overreach
threat_clocks.advances_when: A hero is pushed into situations that their archetype handles poorly, and no ally or resource covers the gap.

yields_resource: A well-matched hero with fitting supplies, and the player's understanding of what each archetype does best.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: Players guide one of three distinct characters through the labyrinthine dungeons and cavernous grottos carved deep in the earth near Tristram. The Sorcerer is one of the playable characters, and the guide advises checking the Witch's supply before other purchases when playing that role. Treat the choice of hero as the opening decision that colors every later problem.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place this at the start of a campaign or descent, before the party enters the dungeon proper. It consumes the table's decision about who plays which archetype and feeds the dungeon module it points to, since the dungeon is where the choice is tested. The Witch's supply is a natural early stop for any Sorcerer. An arrival goes well when each player picks a role with intent and prepares for it. It goes badly when roles are chosen carelessly, or when supplies are neglected and the hero meets the depths unready.

title: Tristram
summary: A medieval village built over a labyrinth of dungeons. It is the party's fixed home base: the dungeon changes, the town does not. Its townsfolk hand out most quests and trade for what the party hauls up from below.
standalone_fallback: Run Tristram as a one-session hub scenario. The party arrives, meets the townsfolk, takes two or three requests tied to something below the town, and has to choose what loot to carry back and what to leave in storage.
premise: A town that depends on adventurers to fetch what it needs + a labyrinth that sits directly beneath its streets = every errand is a bargain with the thing under the church.

sensory.physical_environment: A medieval village with a central fountain, a stream to the southeast, a graveyard, a church with a cursed cathedral, a blacksmith and the witch's hut across the water.
sensory.behaviors: Townsfolk each have something worth saying, ask for items snatched from the dungeon, and trade them for other items or services. Adventurers clean house before hauling goodies back, and drop surplus items on the ground as storage.
sensory.relationships: Cain stands near the fountain. Pepin the Healer and Gillian have houses of their own. Adria the Witch lives across the stream. Ogden keeps the tavern. Wirt whispers for attention behind Gillian's house. All of them depend on whoever goes below.
sensory.attitudes: Hopeful and needy. The townsfolk treat the adventurer as the only one who can fix things, and a wounded townsman begs for help at the cathedral entrance.
sensory.values: Useful trade, practical services, quick cash for unwanted treasure, and a base the party can return to after each excursion.

establishment.name: Cain and the townsfolk
establishment.worldview: The town survives by giving quests to the one who can go below, and by trading fairly with them when they return.
establishment.leverage: They hold the quests, the identification of magical items and the shop inventories.
establishment.flaw: They are helpless without an adventurer and cannot protect the town themselves.

main_opponent.name: The desecrated cathedral
main_opponent.worldview: The church over the dungeon has been turned to something that preys on the town from beneath.
main_opponent.leverage: It is the entry to the labyrinth and the source of the town's troubles.
main_opponent.flaw: It is tied to one place, and the party can always climb back out of it.

thematic_shadow.name: Adria the Witch
thematic_shadow.worldview: Power is a trade good. Knowledge and scrolls are for sale to anyone who brings her something useful.
thematic_shadow.leverage: She supplies healing and mana shield scrolls and buys unwanted treasure.
thematic_shadow.flaw: She lives apart across the stream and is treated warily by the rest of the town.

tertiary_outcast.name: Wirt
tertiary_outcast.worldview: The town ignores him, so he deals quietly with anyone who will listen.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: He whispers offers from behind Gillian's house that others will not make.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: No one trusts him, and he has little of his own to bargain with.

output_dial.level_1: Tristram is a quiet market town where the party trades loot, buys scrolls and collects a few simple requests.
output_dial.level_2: Quests pile up, shop stock is thin, and the party must pick which errands to run and which loot to carry back.
output_dial.level_3: The town is in trouble, with its water poisoned or a great curse spreading, and the townsfolk press the party to act now.
output_dial.level_4: The town is overrun or abandoned, services stop, and whatever is under the church has reached the surface.

threat_clocks.name: The Curse Spreads Through Town
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party ignores the cathedral or the quests it feeds, or comes back empty-handed.

threat_clocks.name: Town Services Collapse
threat_clocks.advances_when: A townsperson is hurt, a shop runs short of stock, or the party fails to deliver what the town asked for.

yields_resource: Quick cash and trade for loot, identification of magical items, healing and mana shield scrolls, free storage of items, and the quests that point toward the dungeon.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: Tristram is the one fixed place in a world of shifting dungeons. The geography of the town does not change while what lies below does. The townsfolk give most of the quests and ask for things taken from the dungeon, then trade them for other items or services. The cathedral is cursed and leads into the labyrinth, and the town sits on top of it all.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place Tristram at the start of the campaign and as the repeated return point between dungeon trips. It consumes dungeon loot and quest results, and feeds back scrolls, identification, quests, storage and rest. It connects to the Cursed Cathedral, the Town Portal, the wider dungeon, the fissure behind Pepin's house and the crypt in the graveyard. An arrival goes well when the party comes in with loot, a clear request and a sense of what to carry. It goes badly when they arrive wounded, with nothing to trade and a town that needs more than they have.

title: Unique Monsters as Ability Tests
summary: A Unique monster serves as a measure of the party: a narrow win means readiness, repeated defeat means something is missing.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a one-shot: a single Unique monster blocks the way forward. How the party fares against it tells them whether to press on, retrain, or change plans entirely.
premise: A party confident in its strength + a Unique that exposes its weak attributes or tactics = a forced reckoning and a change of plan.

sensory.physical_environment: A hard-won clearing where a Unique makes its stand.
sensory.behaviors: The party fights, falls back, regroups, and tries again, or switches approach.
sensory.relationships: Guide to player: advice on reading the outcome; party to Unique: repeated contest.
sensory.attitudes: Frustration giving way to honest self-assessment.
sensory.values: Know your limits; adapt your tactics.

establishment.name: The guide
establishment.worldview: Uniques are a yardstick for readiness.
establishment.leverage: Experience in interpreting how a fight went.
establishment.flaw: Can only advise; cannot fight for the party.

main_opponent.name: The Unique monster
main_opponent.worldview: It simply stands in the way and punishes weakness.
main_opponent.leverage: Strength that outmatches an underprepared party, and resilience against mass magic.
main_opponent.flaw: A change of plan can undo it.

thematic_shadow.name: The overconfident party
thematic_shadow.worldview: Brute repetition will eventually win.
thematic_shadow.leverage: Determination.
thematic_shadow.flaw: Repeats the same failing approach.

tertiary_outcast.name: A party member who spots the pattern early
tertiary_outcast.worldview: Defeat is information, not just failure.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: Insight into what is lacking.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: May not be heeded by the others.

output_dial.level_1: The party barely defeats the Unique and recognizes they are ready to go deeper.
output_dial.level_2: The fight is costly, and the party retreats or rests before a second attempt.
output_dial.level_3: The Unique beats them repeatedly, exposing a gap in strength or tactics they must address.
output_dial.level_4: Stubborn repetition leads to a crushing defeat that forces the party to abandon their plan and rebuild.

threat_clocks.name: Wasted Attempts
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party repeats a failing approach instead of changing tactics, or mass magic fails to hurt the Unique.

yields_resource: Self-knowledge: a clear read on whether the party is ready for the dungeon beyond, and a new plan if not.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: The guide's hint is that Uniques reveal the player's readiness. A barely won fight suggests readiness for what lies ahead; repeated defeat points to a lack in attributes or tactics; a Unique that shrugs off mass magic calls for another plan.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place it as a gatekeeper before a deeper area. It consumes the party's resources and confidence and feeds their decision to advance, retrain, or adapt. It goes well when the party reads the result and changes approach; it goes badly when they keep repeating the same tactic. The Unique itself is not named by the card, so the GM supplies one.

title: Uniques
summary: Named, randomly placed monsters that are devastating versions of ordinary monster types. They resemble their kin apart from coloring or armaments, hit harder and resist more, and lead a horde of more dangerous siblings who share the Unique's special magic until it dies. Slaying one yields a magical item.
standalone_fallback: Run it as a single hunt: the party meets a named, oddly colored brute at the head of an empowered pack in any dark place. They break the pack's borrowed magic by killing the leader, and the leader drops one magical item.
premise: Heroes who need rewards worth the risk + a named brute whose borrowed magic empowers its whole horde = they must decapitate the pack to claim the prize.

sensory.physical_environment: A familiar monster type seen wrong: unusual coloring or armaments, ringed by a pack of ordinary-looking kin that are plainly tougher than they should be.
sensory.behaviors: The horde moves and fights as the Unique's retinue, hitting harder than their kind normally would, while the leader shrugs off attacks that would fell its brethren.
sensory.relationships: Leader and minions are bound by the Unique's special magic ability. The minions hold it only as long as the leader lives.
sensory.attitudes: Dread at a foe that is a devastating version of its kin, set against grim satisfaction that there is a reward for the trouble.
sensory.values: Risk answered by reward: killing the named monster pays out a magical item.

establishment.name: The Unique
establishment.worldview: A named, devastating version of its kin that leads by empowering the horde.
establishment.leverage: Greater punch, more resistances, and a special magic ability shared with its minions.
establishment.flaw: Its horde's power depends wholly on its survival, and its death strips that power away.

main_opponent.name: The adventurers
main_opponent.worldview: A hard fight is worthwhile if the reward is a magical item.
main_opponent.leverage: They can target the leader and break the horde's borrowed magic.
main_opponent.flaw: They must survive the stronger minions and the Unique's resistances long enough to do it.

thematic_shadow.name: The empowered horde
thematic_shadow.worldview: Ordinary kin made more dangerous by a leader's gift.
thematic_shadow.leverage: Numbers and amplified strength.
thematic_shadow.flaw: Their edge is borrowed and vanishes when the Unique dies.

tertiary_outcast.name: Ordinary monsters of the same type
tertiary_outcast.worldview: Plain brethren who lack the leader's mark and share only its shape.
tertiary_outcast.leverage: They are easy to mistake for the Unique's kin and can mask its location.
tertiary_outcast.flaw: They are overshadowed and are the weaker version of their kind.

output_dial.level_1: A named monster is spotted with only a thin escort, a manageable fight that dangles a reward.
output_dial.level_2: The Unique leads a horde of noticeably tougher siblings, and the party must work to reach and fell the leader.
output_dial.level_3: The Unique's resistances and its empowered pack overwhelm a straight fight, forcing the party to retreat, split the horde, or find a way to isolate the leader.
output_dial.level_4: A Unique with a lethal magic ability and a large horde corners the party, and every minion fights with borrowed power until the leader is somehow brought down.

threat_clocks.name: The Horde Closes In
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party lingers in the open, fights the minions piecemeal, or fails to locate the Unique.

threat_clocks.name: Borrowed Power Holds
threat_clocks.advances_when: The party's attacks are wasted on resistant targets or the Unique stays shielded behind its minions.

yields_resource: A magical item from the slain Unique, plus the collapse of the horde's special magic.

sections.heading: Core Premise
sections.text: A Unique is a named, randomly placed monster that is a devastating version of an ordinary type. It looks like its kin apart from coloring or armaments, hits harder, resists more, and usually leads more dangerous ordinary siblings. It grants its horde its special magic ability, and the minions lose that ability when it dies. Killing it rewards the party with a magical item.

sections.heading: GM Placement & Synergies
sections.text: Place a Unique as a mid-delve encounter in any area where ordinary monsters of its type already live, so the contrast is obvious. It consumes the party's resources and attention and feeds them a magical item, which can tie into item-property hooks. An arrival goes well when the party spots the unusual coloring early, targets the leader, and watches the horde falter. It goes badly when they treat it as a routine fight, meet the leader's resistances unprepared, and are ground down by empowered minions.
